x and y are the points being compared, m is the number of dimensions, and x_i and y_i are the coordinates of the points in the i-th dimension
This measure is distinct from similarity scores, such as cosine similarity, where larger values indicate greater similarity, whereas Manhattan distance is a distance metric.
The value of Manhattan distance is always non-negative and finite, satisfying the condition 0 ≤ d_Manhattan(x, y) < ∞
In the context of clustering, when the objective is to minimize the sum of distances, the appropriate centroid for a cluster using Manhattan distance is the median of the points in that cluster
Cosine similarity is a similarity score, distinct from distance measures like Manhattan and Euclidean distance, where a larger value indicates greater similarity.
It measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors, x and y.
When the cosine similarity is 1, the angle between the vectors is 0 degrees, meaning they point in the same direction and are identical except for length.
When the cosine similarity is 0, the angle is 90 degrees, indicating the vectors are perpendicular and do not share any terms.
When the cosine similarity is -1, the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.
The calculation involves normalizing the vectors by dividing them by their lengths, which results in vectors of length 1.
This normalization means cosine similarity does not take the length of the data objects into account.
For unit-length vectors, the cosine measure is calculated by taking a simple inner product.
This approach is useful for sparse data, such as documents represented as vectors where components record word frequencies, and can reduce computation time when many similarities are calculated.
In the context of clustering, cosine similarity is used as a proximity measure in K-means style algorithms, where the objective is to maximize the similarity of objects to the cluster centroid.
It is also included in the class of Bregman divergences, which can serve as the basis for clustering algorithms with convergence properties similar to standard K-means.
The Rand Index is an external validation measure used to evaluate clustering by comparing the cluster structure against true class labels.
It is a similarity-oriented measure that operates by comparing pairs of objects.
The index is calculated using the formula: Rand Index = (f11 + f00) / (f11 + f10 + f01 + f00).
In this formula, f00 represents the pairs of objects that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering.

The Rand Index includes these f00 pairs in its calculation, which distinguishes it from the Jaccard Coefficient, a sibling measure that ignores f00 and focuses only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
Consequently, the Rand Index is often higher than the Jaccard Coefficient.
The calculation counts only pairs of distinct objects; self-pairs are not included in the Rand Index computation.
The Rand Index does not require the original feature values once the cluster assignments and class labels are available.
It is computed through class similarity and cluster similarity matrices.
An adjusted version of the Rand Index exists and is based on the multivariate hypergeometric distribution, which can be used to compute a p-value.

The Jaccard coefficient is a similarity measure used to evaluate the similarity between two binary vectors, particularly in contexts involving asymmetric binary attributes such as transaction data where a 1 indicates an item was purchased and a 0 indicates it was not.
It is frequently employed as a cluster validity measure and is often symbolized by j.
The coefficient is defined by the formula Jaccard Coefficient = f11 / (f11 + f10 + f01), where f11, f10, and f01 represent specific frequency counts from a contingency table.
A key characteristic of the Jaccard coefficient is that it ignores f00, focusing only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
This distinguishes it from other measures like the Rand statistic (or Simple Matching Coefficient), which includes f00 in its calculation.
For example, given f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Jaccard coefficient is calculated as 2 / (2 + 2 + 2) = 0.33.

The measure can be extended to more than two variables using multidimensional contingency tables, and an extended version, known as the Extended Jaccard Coefficient or Tanimoto Coefficient, is used for document data and reduces to the standard Jaccard coefficient for binary attributes.
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set.
The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity.
Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity.
This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.
In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix.
The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise.

When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere.
The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.
The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results.
By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters.
For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks.

Additionally, in supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient.
In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.
A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset.

Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect.
Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible.
The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used.

Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing, though this can be inaccurate if the frequency of missing values depends on the class label.
Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect.
logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded.

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on probability; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a surrogate attribute; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value.
General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation.
Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical.
Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes).
There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.
A missingness mechanism describes the underlying process that determines which values in a dataset are missing.

Categorizing these mechanisms is a critical step in data preprocessing because the assumptions made about the missingness mechanism and the pattern of missing values directly affect which treatment methods can be correctly applied.
The evidence specifically defines the Missing at Random (MAR) mechanism.
In the MAR case, the probability that an observation is missing may depend on the observed part of the data (Xobs) but not on the missing part (Xmis).

Formally, if X is partitioned into Xobs and Xmis, the MAR assumption implies that the distribution of the missingness indicator B, given Xobs and Xmis, is identical to the distribution of B given only Xobs.
P(B|Xobs, Xmis, ζ) = P(B|Xobs, ζ), where B is an n × p matrix of indicators (1 for observed, 0 for missing) and ζ represents unknown parameters.
This is expressed by the equation P(B|Xobs, Xmis, ζ) = P(B|Xobs, ζ), where B is an n × p matrix of indicators (1 for observed, 0 for missing) and ζ represents unknown parameters.
This means that for a given set of observed features, the distribution of the remaining features is the same among observed cases as it is among missing cases.

The choice of missingness mechanism is also a prerequisite for specific imputation techniques; for instance, Multiple Imputation (MI) is only applicable when the data follows a Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) or MAR mechanism.
Simple imputation methods often ignore the missingness mechanism entirely, whereas advanced methods require this categorization to function correctly.
The Deletion Strategy is a data preprocessing approach that handles missing values by eliminating data objects or attributes that contain them.
A simple and effective strategy is to eliminate objects with missing values.
This approach is considered expedient when a data set has only a few objects that have missing values.
even a partially specified data object contains some information, and if many objects have missing values, then a reliable analysis can be difficult or impossible.
A related strategy is to eliminate attributes that have missing values.
the eliminated attributes may be the ones that are critical to the analysis.
Imputation is the process of replacing missing values (MVs) in a dataset with estimated values.

It is distinguished from deletion strategies, which remove cases containing missing data, and from the classification of missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, NMAR), which describe how data is lost rather than how to fill it.

The goal of imputation is to obtain values for non-reference attributes (attributes with missing values) for incomplete objects, using the available reference attributes (attributes with known values).
Imputation methods generally fall into two broad categories: statistical methods and machine learning (ML) methods.
Statistical methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Imputation and Expectation-Maximization (EM), model the underlying probability distribution of the data.

EM algorithms, often used with Gaussian mixture models, iteratively estimate parameters like the mean (μ) and covariance (Σ) to impute missing values via regression.

Machine learning methods, such as K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI) and Fuzzy K-means Imputation, do not require assuming a specific underlying distribution but still rely on the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption.

KMI works by clustering data into K groups, where each cluster is represented by a centroid. The algorithm proceeds in three steps: (1) randomly select K complete data objects as initial centroids; (2) iteratively update the partition to minimize the sum of distances between objects and their assigned centroids until a threshold ε is met or centroids stabilize; and (3) impute missing values for incomplete objects using the cluster information, treating objects in the same cluster as nearest neig

Fuzzy K-means imputation extends this by allowing objects to belong to multiple clusters with different membership degrees, calculating imputed values as a weighted sum of cluster centroids based on these memberships.
Other approaches include Support Vector Machines Imputation (SVMI) and Hot Deck imputation, which is a historical method used by the Census Bureau.
Evaluating imputation methods is challenging.
In unsupervised settings, Mean Squared Error (MSE) or Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) are commonly used to compare imputed values against known true values (by artificially introducing missingness).
In supervised settings, such as classification, the goal is to improve classifier accuracy, which is harder to measure directly with MSE/RMSE.
Metrics like Wilson’s Noise Ratio may be used to assess the impact of imputation on the learning task.
Data integration is the process of merging data elements from different sources into a single data set.
This task is required when there are several or heterogeneous sources of data, as gathering all data elements together is not an easy task.

Different attribute names or table schemes from various sources produce uneven examples that need to be consolidated, and attribute values may represent the same concept with different names, creating inconsistencies in the instances obtained.
An essential part of the integration process is to build a data map that establishes how each instance should be arranged in a common structure to present a real-world example.
When data is obtained from relational databases, it is usually flattened and gathered together into one single record.
Some database frameworks enable the user to provide a map to directly traverse the database through in-database access utilities.
While using in-database mining tools has the advantage of not having to extract and create an external file for the data, it is not the best option for its treatment with preprocessing techniques.
In this case, extracting the data is usually the best option.
Preprocessing takes time, and when the data is kept in the database, preprocessing has to be applied repeatedly.
If the data is extracted to an external file, then processing and modeling it can be faster if the data is already preprocessed and completely fits in memory.
If the integration process is not properly performed, redundancies and inconsistencies will soon appear, resulting in a decrease of the accuracy and speed of the subsequent data mining processes.

Matching the schema from different sources presents a notorious problem that usually does not come alone: inconsistent and duplicated tuples as well as redundant and correlated attributes are problems that the data set creation process will probably show sooner or later.
Automatic approaches used to integrate the data can be found in the literature, from techniques that match and find the schemas of the data to automatic procedures that reconcile different schemas.
After the data is correctly integrated into a data set, it does not mean that the data is free from errors.
The integration may result in an inordinate proportion of the data being dirty.
Broadly, dirty data include missing data, wrong data and non-standard representation of the same data.
If a high proportion of the data is dirty, applying a data mining process will surely result in an unreliable model.
Dirty data has varying degrees of impact depending on the data mining algorithm, but it is difficult to quantify such an impact.
An attribute is redundant when it can be derived from another attribute or set of them, or when it is strongly correlated with another attribute in the data.

Redundancy is a problem that should be avoided as much as possible because it usually causes an increment in the data set size, meaning that the modeling time of data mining algorithms is incremented as well, and may also induce overfitting in the obtained model.
Inconsistencies in dimension or attribute names can cause redundancies as well.

When examples come from different sources and have to be merged in a single data set, if some attributes are calculated from the others, the data sets will present a large size but the information contained will not scale accordingly, making detecting and eliminating redundant attributes needed.
Redundancies in attributes can be detected using correlation analysis, which measures how strong the implication of one attribute to the other is.
When the data is nominal and the set of values is finite, the chi-squared test is commonly applied.
In numeric attributes, the use of the correlation coefficient and the covariance is typical.

For two nominal attributes A and B containing c and r distinct values each, a contingency table is created with the joint events (Ai, Bj) in which attribute A takes the value ai and attribute B takes the value bj.

The chi-squared value is computed as the sum over i from 1 to c and j from 1 to r of (oij - eij)^2 / eij, where oij is the observed frequency of the joint event (Ai, Bj) and eij is the expected frequency of (Ai, Bj) computed as count(A = ai) × count(B = bj) / m.

Here, m is the number of instances in the data set, count(A = ai) is the number of instances with the value ai for attribute A, and count(B = bj) is the number of instances having the value bj for attribute B.
The chi-squared test checks the hypothesis that A and B are independent, with (r-1) × (c-1) degrees of freedom.
The chi-squared statistic is compared against a chi-squared table using the suitable degrees of freedom or available software.

If the significance level of the table is below the established one, or the statistic value computed is above the needed one in the table, the null hypothesis is rejected and A and B are statistically correlated.

For two numerical attributes, the correlation coefficient rA,B is computed as the sum over i from 1 to m of (ai - A_bar)(bi - B_bar) / (m σA σB), which is equivalent to (sum over i from 1 to m of (ai bi) - m A_bar B_bar) / (m σA σB).

Here, m is the number of instances, ai and bi are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A_bar and B_bar are the mean values of A and B respectively, and σA and σB are the standard deviations of A and B.
Checking whether numerical attributes are highly correlated is useful to determine if they are redundant.
Different classifiers handle redundant attributes in different ways.

Decision trees can handle the presence of redundant attributes because redundant attributes show similar gains in purity if they are selected for splitting, so only one of them will be selected as an attribute test condition.

Logistic regression can handle redundant attributes that are duplicates of each other by learning equal weights for every redundant attribute without degrading classification performance, although a large number of irrelevant or redundant attributes in high-dimensional settings can make it susceptible to model overfitting.

Linear SVM can handle redundant attributes by learning similar weights for the duplicate attributes, and its ability to regularize its learning makes it more robust to the presence of a large number of irrelevant and redundant attributes than other classifiers.

Rule-based classifiers can easily handle the presence of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with one other because once an attribute has been used as a conjunct in a rule antecedent, the remaining redundant attributes would show little to no information gain and would thus be ignored.

Bayesian networks can easily handle the presence of correlated or redundant attributes because they do not use the naive Bayes assumption about conditional independence, but instead are able to express richer forms of conditional independence.

Artificial neural networks can handle redundant attributes by receiving similar weights for them without degrading the quality of the classifier, although if the number of irrelevant or redundant attributes is large, the learning of the ANN model may suffer from overfitting.

The presence of a large number of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with each other can bias proximity measures toward such attributes, resulting in improper estimates of distance and adversely affecting the performance of nearest neighbor classifiers.
Duplicate tuples are repeated instances of data records that appear in a dataset, often arising from the use of denormalized tables or errors in the data entry process.
These duplicates are a significant concern in data preprocessing because they waste storage space and computing time for data mining algorithms and can serve as a source of inconsistency.

A particularly difficult case occurs when entry errors cause slight differences in attribute values, such as identifier values, resulting in instances that are substantively identical but are treated as distinct; these are harder to detect than simple exact matches.

Duplicate tuples frequently emerge during the data integration process, where matching schemas from different sources can introduce redundancies and inconsistencies that degrade the accuracy and speed of subsequent data mining tasks.
While the source material identifies the detection of tuple duplication as a specific preprocessing step, it does not provide a formal algorithm or procedure for resolving these duplicates.
Inconsistent values are data quality issues where recorded attribute values differ from the true values or violate established constraints.
This can occur when information is sourced from different systems with varying measurement standards, leading to instances that are actually the same but not identified as such.
A specific form of inconsistency arises when attribute values fall outside the established range, a condition usually indicated in the associated metadata for the data set.
A common example is an address field where the specified zip code area is not contained within the listed city, which may result from transposed digits or misread handwritten forms.
In the context of duplicate detection, inconsistent values must be resolved when two objects represent a single entity but have differing attribute values.
It is important to detect and, if possible, correct such problems to ensure data integrity.
Data cleaning is the first step in data preprocessing, specifically defined as the detection and correction of data inaccuracies.
It is a necessary phase that occurs after data has become computer-readable and constitutes a unique source, but before any data mining (DM) technique is applied.
The primary goal of data cleaning is to filter or repair dirty data to ensure that the knowledge extracted by DM algorithms is accurate and that the algorithms can effectively handle the data.
Without this step, the presence of dirty data can lead to less reliable models or prevent algorithms from functioning properly.
Dirty data typically manifests in two main forms: missing data and wrong (noisy) data.
The sources of these errors include data entry errors, data update errors, data transmission errors, and bugs in the data processing system.
It is important to distinguish data cleaning from other preprocessing steps; for instance, having a uniform data set without measurable inconsistencies does not automatically mean the data is clean.

Furthermore, data cleaning is distinct from data normalization and transformation, which are used to adapt the data set to the specific needs of the DM algorithm (such as handling nominal attributes or subtle transformations) rather than correcting inaccuracies.

The impact of dirty data varies by algorithm; for example, decision trees (especially those of higher order), artificial neural networks (ANNs), and distance-based algorithms like KNN are known to be susceptible to noise.
Therefore, data cleaning is a foundational technique required to improve the accuracy and efficiency of subsequent data mining processes.
Normalization and transformation are data preprocessing techniques used to adapt a data set to the needs of a subsequent data mining algorithm.
A variable transformation is a transformation applied to all the values of a variable, meaning that for each object, the transformation is applied to the value of the variable for that object.
if only the magnitude of a variable is important, the values can be transformed by taking the absolute value.
'normalization' usually refers to a particular case of min-max normalization in which the final interval is [0, 1], meaning the new minimum is 0 and the new maximum is 1.
The interval [-1, 1] is also typical when normalizing data.
v' = new-min_A + R * ((v - min_A) / (max_A - min_A)), where max_A and min_A are the original maximum and minimum attribute values respectively.

Rescaling all data to the same range of values avoids attributes with a large max_A - min_A difference dominating over others in distance calculations, which would otherwise mislead the learning process by giving more importance to those attributes.
Normalization is also known for speeding up the learning process in artificial neural networks (ANNs), helping weights to converge faster.

In some cases, transformation or normalization of the data is needed to obtain a proper similarity measure, such as when time series have trends or periodic patterns that significantly impact similarity.

A specific transformation useful for obtaining a new variable that is very likely to behave like a normally distributed one involves using the rank of the observation and the cumulative normal function.
However, this transformation cannot be applied separately to the training and test partitions; it is only recommended when the test and training data is the same.
A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against the true labels of instances in a test set.
It is the most basic approach for representing classification performance and provides a concise, detailed representation of how a model predicts correctly or incorrectly.
For a binary classification problem, the matrix is organized with rows representing the true class and columns representing the predicted class.

It contains four specific counts: True Positives (TP), which are actual positives predicted as positive; False Negatives (FN), which are actual positives predicted as negative; False Positives (FP), which are actual negatives predicted as positive; and True Negatives (TN), which are actual negatives predicted as negative.
The confusion matrix is used to evaluate models trained on independent training and test sets to ensure accurate prediction of unseen instances.

While the matrix provides the necessary information to determine model performance, it is often difficult to interpret and compare classifiers using the four-dimensional representation of these counts.
Consequently, the counts are often summarized into single-value evaluation measures, such as accuracy, to facilitate the comparison of relative performance between different models.
The confusion matrix is also applicable in contexts such as clustering, where it provides the most detailed information for evaluating the performance of a specific cluster against a class.
Accuracy is a metric used to evaluate the quality of classification rules and classifiers.

In the context of a specific classification rule, accuracy (also referred to as the confidence factor) is defined as the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels are equal to the predicted class.

For binary classification, accuracy is calculated as the sum of true positives and true negatives divided by the total number of predictions (true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives).
It can also be expressed generally as the number of correct predictions divided by the number of all predictions.
Accuracy is an estimate based on a finite test set and is not guaranteed to be the exact true accuracy of the classifier.
A higher raw accuracy alone is not always a significant win; a raw accuracy difference is not automatically a significant win.
Accuracy can be misleading because it can hide poor positive-class performance, especially under class imbalance.
Larger test sets reduce sampling uncertainty associated with the measured accuracy.
Precision is an evaluation measure for binary classification that quantifies the fraction of correct predictions of the positive class over the total number of positive predictions.
It is also referred to as the positive predicted value (PPV).
The standard formula for precision is p = TP / (TP + FP), where TP represents true positives and FP represents false positives.

A classifier with high precision is likely to have most of its positive predictions correct, making it a useful measure for highly skewed test sets where positive predictions, even though small in numbers, are required to be mostly correct.

Precision is sensitive to class skew; when selecting a score threshold for a classifier, if the evaluation measure is precision, the skew of the validation set used for selection must be similar to that of the test set to ensure optimal performance.
In the context of statistical testing, precision is closely related to the false discovery rate (FDR), with the relationship precision = 1 - FDR.

Precision captures the effect of false positives but not false negatives; a classifier that is very conservative in classifying instances as positive to reduce false positives may end up having high precision but very poor recall.
A perfect classifier is characterized by precision = 1 and recall = 1.
Recall, also known as sensitivity in the medical community, is a classifier evaluation metric that measures the proportion of actual positive instances correctly identified by the model.
It is defined by the formula Recall = TP / (TP + FN), where TP represents true positives and FN represents false negatives.
A classifier with a high recall value has a high chance of correctly identifying the positive instances in the data.
In the information retrieval literature, this metric is also referred to as recall (r).

This metric is distinct from precision, which is based on predicted positives, and specificity, which is based on actual negatives.
Specificity, also known as the true negative rate (TNR), is a classifier evaluation metric defined as the fraction of negative test instances correctly predicted by the classifier.
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)
This metric specifically checks how many actual negatives were correctly rejected by the model.
It is distinct from precision for the negative class because specificity uses actual negatives in the denominator, whereas negative predictive value uses predicted negatives.

Specificity is used alongside other metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F-measure to provide a comprehensive view of classifier performance, particularly when the correct rejection of negative cases is a priority.
