Comparing two models on independent test sets is a statistical evaluation task used to determine whether the observed difference in performance between two classification models is statistically significant.
a simple comparison of accuracy or error rates can be misleading, particularly when the models are evaluated on test sets of different sizes
a model achieving 85% accuracy on a test set of 30 instances may not be statistically superior to a model achieving 75% accuracy on a test set of 5,000 instances
The standard setup for this comparison involves two models, denoted as M1 and M2, which are evaluated on two independent test sets, D1 and D2.
The number of instances in each test set is denoted as n1 and n2, respectively.
The error rate for model M1 on test set D1 is denoted as e1, and the error rate for model M2 on test set D2 is denoted as e2
The primary goal of this unit is to test whether the observed difference between e1 and e2 is statistically significant

This unit is distinct from specific statistical tests such as the McNemar test or the Friedman test, which are used for different evaluation scenarios, such as paired comparisons or multiple model comparisons
The significance level, denoted by the Greek letter alpha (α), is a fixed constant in hypothesis testing whose value is decided before any tests are performed.
It is defined as the probability of incurring a type I error, which is equal to the probability of the critical region under the null hypothesis.
In practice, a result is called statistically significant if it has a p-value lower than the pre-specified threshold α.

This threshold is equivalent to the boundary of the critical region; rejecting the null hypothesis if the test statistic falls in the critical region is equivalent to rejecting it if the p-value falls below α.
While every result has a different p-value, the significance level remains a fixed constant for the testing procedure.
Common choices for the level of significance are 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%).

In specific applications, such as a one-sided test, the significance level determines the critical value used for decision-making; for example, at a significance level of 0.05, the critical value for a one-sided test is Z = 1.64.

The significance level also serves as the target for controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) in multiple testing scenarios, where procedures like Bonferroni adjust the per-test significance level to ensure the overall FWER remains below α.
In the context of model evaluation, one-sided and two-sided tests are statistical procedures used to determine whether an observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis.
The test statistic, typically a count or real-valued quantity, measures how 'extreme' an observed result is under the null hypothesis.
One-sided tests are categorized as right-tailed or left-tailed, while two-sided tests evaluate whether the result is extreme in either direction.

The distinction is reflected in the distribution of the significance level (alpha) across the tails of the null distribution: a two-sided test with an alpha of 0.05 allocates 0.025 probability to each tail, whereas a one-sided test allocates the entire 0.05 probability to a single tail.
A low p-value indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution, providing sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

For example, a one-sided test asking whether model A is better than model B is distinct from a two-tailed test, which asks whether the classifiers are different in either direction and would normally use a threshold of |Z| > 1.96 at alpha = 0.05.
The role of test sample size in model evaluation is defined by the direct dependence of measured accuracy on the specific test sample used.

When selecting a sample size, there is a fundamental trade-off: larger sample sizes increase the probability that the sample will be representative of the underlying data, but they also eliminate much of the computational advantage of sampling.
Conversely, smaller sample sizes carry the risk that true patterns can be missed or that erroneous patterns can be detected.

This impact on representativeness is demonstrated by a data set containing 8000 two-dimensional points, where a sample of 2000 points preserves most of the structure, whereas a sample of 500 points misses much of it.

In a specific clustering context, a sample size of 20 has a 20% chance of failing to include all 10 clusters, and a sample size of 30 still has an almost 40% chance of missing objects from all 10 clusters.
These examples illustrate that sample size directly determines the reliability of the evaluation metric.
An ensemble classifier is a method that constructs a set of base classifiers from training data and performs classification by taking a vote on the predictions made by each base classifier.
The base classifiers are often individually imperfect, but their combined decision can be more robust.
For classification, a common combination rule is majority voting, where the final prediction is determined by the majority of the individual predictions.
An alternate approach is to take a weighted majority vote, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance.
The ensemble classifier predicts the class label of a test example by taking a majority vote on the predictions made by the base classifiers.
If the base classifiers are identical, then all the base classifiers will commit the same mistakes, and the error rate of the ensemble remains the same as the individual classifiers.
If the base classifiers are independent—i.e., their errors are uncorrelated—then the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly.
In this case, the error rate of the ensemble classifier is lower than that of the individual classifiers.
The ensemble classifier performs worse than the base classifiers when the base classifier error rate is larger than 0.5.

Two necessary conditions for an ensemble classifier to perform better than a single classifier are: (1) the base classifiers should be independent of each other, and (2) the base classifiers should do better than a classifier that performs random guessing.

In practice, it is difficult to ensure total independence among the base classifiers, but improvements in classification accuracies have been observed in ensemble methods in which the base classifiers are somewhat correlated.

The ensemble of classifiers can be constructed in many ways, including by manipulating the training set, where multiple training sets are created by resampling the original data according to some sampling distribution and constructing a classifier from each training set.
Bagging and boosting are two examples of ensemble methods that manipulate their training sets.
The base classifiers for most of these approaches can be generated sequentially (one after another) or in parallel (all at once).
Once an ensemble of classifiers has been learned, a test example is classified by combining the predictions made by the base classifiers.
The final prediction of the ensemble classifier is obtained by taking a weighted average of the predictions made by each base classifier.

The ensemble classifier can also enhance the representation of the target function; even though each base classifier is a decision stump, combining the classifiers can lead to a decision boundary that mimics a decision tree of depth 2.

The ensemble classifier is a general method that can be applied to any classifier, and it is used to improve the performance of a single classifier by combining the predictions of multiple base classifiers.
Majority voting is a combination rule used in ensemble classification to derive a single final prediction from the outputs of multiple base classifiers.
each base classifier predicts a class label for a given instance, and the final prediction is the class that receives the most votes
This method is particularly common in random forests, where the final prediction is obtained by majority voting over the individual decision trees.

The ensemble is strongest when the individual trees are reasonably accurate and their errors are not perfectly correlated, as this diversity helps reduce the high variance associated with single decision trees.
A weighted majority vote is an alternative approach where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance, but in standard majority voting, every vote has equal impact.
In the context of k-nearest neighbors, majority voting assigns the test instance to the majority class of its nearest neighbors, with ties potentially resolved by random choice.
The procedure involves sending a test instance through all base classifiers or trees and combining their predictions using this voting mechanism.
A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees, where each tree is trained using randomness so that the trees are not all identical.
The method manipulates both the training instances and the input features to create diversity among the base classifiers.
The training data is represented as a set of instances D = {(x1, y1), (x2, y2), ..., (xN, yN)}
The induction process for each tree b = 1, 2, ..., B involves drawing a bootstrap sample Db from the original training set by sampling N instances with replacement.
A decision tree is then trained on Db, often grown deeply and without heavy pruning, meaning the trees are unpruned and allowed to grow until every leaf is pure.
At every split, the tree considers only a random subset of features and chooses the best split from that subset.
The number of attributes to be selected at every node, p, is a hyper-parameter of the random forest classifier.

For classification, the final prediction is made by combining the trees using majority voting: ŷ = majority{h1(x), h2(x), ..., hB(x)}, where x is the test instance, hb is the b-th base classifier, and ŷ is the final ensemble prediction.
The two main random components are bootstrap sampling of instances and random feature selection at each split.
This approach reduces the variance of the trees without negatively impacting their low bias, making random forests robust to overfitting and computationally fast even in high-dimensional settings.
Boosting is an iterative ensemble procedure that adaptively changes the distribution of training examples so that base classifiers increasingly focus on examples that are hard to classify.
Unlike bagging, boosting assigns a weight to each training example and may adaptively change the weight at the end of each boosting round.
The algorithm begins by assigning equal weights to all examples, then draws a sample according to the sampling distribution to obtain a new training set.
A classifier is built from this training set and used to classify all examples in the original data.

At the end of each boosting round, the weights of the training examples are updated: examples that are classified incorrectly have their weights increased, while those classified correctly have their weights decreased.
As the boosting rounds proceed, examples that are the hardest to classify tend to become even more prevalent in the sampling distribution.
The final ensemble is obtained by aggregating the base classifiers obtained from each boosting round.
In the AdaBoost implementation, the prediction made by each classifier is weighted rather than using a majority voting scheme, which allows the algorithm to penalize models that have poor accuracy.
If any intermediate round produces an error rate higher than 50%, the weights are reverted back to their original uniform values and the resampling procedure is repeated.

The training error of the ensemble decreases exponentially, leading to fast convergence, although the technique can be susceptible to overfitting due to its tendency to focus on wrongly classified examples.
The class imbalance problem is a practical issue in classification where the training set has an unbalanced representation of classes, typically with a minority class that is not well-represented.

This imbalance poses two challenges for classification: first, many classification methods work well only when the training set has a balanced representation of both classes, and second, a classifier trained over an imbalanced data set shows a bias toward improving its performance over the majority class, which is often not the desired behavior.
In the context of binary classification, the minority class is referred to as the positive class, while the majority class is referred to as the negative class.
The problem is particularly relevant in model evaluation, where detection rate and false alarm rate are metrics that are not sensitive to skewness in the class distribution.

In the presence of class imbalance, the behavior of an algorithm over small false positive rate values (also termed as early retrieval) is often more meaningful for comparison than the performance over all false positive rate values.
in many applications, it is important to assess the true positive rate achieved by a classifier in the first few instances with highest scores, without incurring a large false positive rate.
The precision-recall (PR) curve is an alternate approach for measuring the aggregate performance of a classifier, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance.

The PR curve generally helps to magnify the differences between classifiers in the left portion of the PR curve, providing a deeper insight into the performance of classifiers than the ROC curves, especially in the early retrieval range of operating points.
Oversampling is a technique used to create a balanced training set by artificially generating new positive examples to address class imbalance.

A simple approach involves duplicating every positive instance a specific number of times, where the duplication factor is determined by the ratio of the number of negative training instances to the number of positive training instances.

This duplication method is analogous to doubling the weight of positive instances during the training stage, an effect that can alternatively be achieved by assigning higher weights to positive instances than negative instances, a method compatible with classifiers such as logistic regression, artificial neural networks, and support vector machines.

However, a limitation of the duplication method is that replicated positive examples have an artificially lower variance compared to their true distribution, which can bias the classifier to the specific distribution of training instances and lead to poor generalizability.
To overcome this limitation, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) generates synthetic positive instances in the neighborhood of existing positive instances.

The SMOTE procedure first determines the k-nearest positive neighbors of every positive instance, then generates a synthetic positive instance at some intermediate point along the line segment joining the instance to one of its randomly chosen k-nearest neighbors.
This process is repeated until the desired number of positive instances is reached.

A limitation of SMOTE is that it can only generate new positive instances within the convex hull of the existing positive class, meaning it does not improve the representation of the positive class outside the boundary of existing positive instances.
Despite their complementary strengths and weaknesses, undersampling and oversampling provide useful directions for generating balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance.

Undersampling is a sampling method used to create balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance by reducing the frequency of the majority class to match the frequency of the minority class.

This approach is one of two primary strategies for ensuring that a learning algorithm is trained over a data set with adequate representation of both the majority and minority classes, the other being oversampling.
To illustrate the procedure, consider a training set containing 100 positive examples and 1000 negative examples.
To overcome the skew among the classes, a random sample of 100 examples is selected from the negative class and used with the 100 positive examples to create a balanced training set.
One limitation is that some useful negative examples, particularly those closer to the actual decision boundary, may not be chosen for training, which can result in an inferior classification model.
Another limitation is that the smaller sample of negative instances may have a higher variance than the larger original set.
Undersampling and oversampling provide complementary directions for generating balanced training sets, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses.
The cost matrix is a tool for evaluating cost-sensitive decision quality by assigning specific costs to different types of classification decisions.
It is used to determine the best model based on the real consequences of each type of decision, rather than relying solely on standard metrics like ROC/AUC or F1.
In a cost-sensitive setting, the model with the lowest expected cost is selected as the best.
For example, in a specific exercise, model M3 was identified as the best because it had the lowest expected cost, even though other models performed better on ROC/AUC and F1 metrics.
The expected cost per instance is calculated using the prior probability, false positive rate, true positive rate, and the cost matrix.
In one instance, the expected cost per instance was 0.390 under a prior probability of 0.1.
The cost matrix can include negative costs for true positives, which reduce the total cost.
The cost of a model and data is defined as the sum of the cost of the data given the model and a weighted cost of the model itself, where the weight is a parameter alpha.
The cost of a tree and data is defined as the sum of the cost of the tree and the cost of the data given the tree.
The cost matrix is distinct from the confusion matrix, which is a related but different concept.
Cost-Sensitive Classification is an approach to model evaluation and learning that accounts for the differing consequences of misclassification errors.
It is motivated by the need for evaluation metrics that are sensitive to class skew and capture performance criteria beyond simple accuracy.
The method involves evaluating decision quality using a cost matrix, where the choice of a model is determined by minimizing the expected cost.
In a specific evaluation context, a model was selected based on having the lowest expected cost of 0.390.

The foundations of this area include the study of cost matrix properties and various methods for incorporating cost information into learning algorithms, such as wrapper methods, class distribution-based methods, and loss-based methods.
Algorithm-independent methods include AdaCost, MetaCost, and costing.
Cost-sensitive boosting is also a recognized technique in this domain.

RIPPER is a widely-used rule induction algorithm that implements a direct method for generating classification rules directly from data, distinguishing it from indirect methods that derive rules from decision trees.
It is designed to work well with noisy data by using a validation set to prevent model overfitting.
The algorithm typically employs a sequential covering scheme to induce rules.
After generating a rule, RIPPER eliminates all positive and negative examples covered by that rule.
The rule is added to the rule set provided it does not violate specific stopping conditions.

One stopping condition is based on the minimum description length principle: if a new rule increases the total description length of the rule set by at least d bits, RIPPER stops adding rules; by default, d is chosen to be 64 bits.
Another stopping condition requires that the error rate of the rule on the validation set must not exceed 50%.
RIPPER also prunes rules to improve generalization errors based on their performance on the validation set.
Pruning is done starting from the last conjunct added to the rule, removing a conjunct if a specific metric improves after pruning.
This metric is monotonically related to the rule's accuracy on the validation set and involves the number of positive and negative examples in the validation set covered by the rule.
While the original rule covers only positive examples, the pruned rule may cover some negative examples in the training set.
The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is a widely used graphical tool for aggregate evaluation of classifiers.
It displays the trade-off between the true positive rate (TPR) and the false positive rate (FPR) across varying score thresholds.
In this plot, the TPR is positioned on the y-axis and the FPR on the x-axis.
Each point on the curve represents a specific operating point of the classifier, generated by applying a particular threshold to the test scores produced by the model.

Because every point corresponds to a different threshold, the curve facilitates the comparison of classifiers over a range of operating points, allowing users to select a threshold based on application requirements.
The generic procedure for computing an ROC curve involves sorting the predictions according to their score values and then plotting the TPR and FPR for every possible value of the score threshold.

This approach allows for the empirical estimation of classification performance for different score thresholds in the presence of ground truth labels, without requiring explicit statistical models or assumptions.

The resulting curve typically exhibits a staircase pattern because the TPR monotonically increases with FPR; as instances are included in the set of predicted positives, the TPR or FPR increases, but not both simultaneously.
A random classifier, which performs random guessing, resides at the point (p, p) along the main diagonal of the ROC curve, where p represents the probability of correct classification.
A perfect classifier, which correctly classifies all instances, corresponds to the top-left corner of the plot.
A good ROC curve is characterized by rising quickly before moving far to the right, indicating that the model catches positives before creating many false positives.
Conversely, a curve closer to the top-left corner represents better performance.

While the area under the ROC curve (AUC) is a common summary measure, the ROC curve itself provides the detailed view of performance across all operating points, which is essential when comparing classifiers that may intersect or dominate each other only in specific ranges of FPR.
ROC Space (TPR vs. FPR) is the two-dimensional coordinate system used to visualize the trade-off between a classifier's True Positive Rate (TPR) and False Positive Rate (FPR).
In this space, the TPR is plotted along the y-axis and the FPR is shown on the x-axis.
Each point in this space corresponds to a specific classification model generated by placing a threshold on the test scores produced by the classifier.

The space is bounded by four critical points: (TPR=0, FPR=0) represents a model that predicts every instance as negative; (TPR=1, FPR=0) represents the perfect model with zero misclassifications; (TPR=1, FPR=1) represents a model that predicts every instance as positive; and (TPR=0, FPR=1) represents a model that predicts every instance as negative while misclassifying all positives.

A model that makes random guesses resides along the main diagonal connecting (TPR=0, FPR=0) and (TPR=1, FPR=1), where the TPR and FPR are equal to the fixed probability p of classifying an instance as positive.
A good classification model is located as close as possible to the upper left corner of the diagram.
The ROC curve, which traces the path of these points as the threshold varies, exhibits a staircase pattern because the TPR monotonically increases with FPR.
ROC Space is agnostic to the skew in the test set because both TPR and FPR are invariant to class imbalance; consequently, the same ROC curve is obtained for test data sets with very different skew.

This characteristic makes ROC Space unsuitable for measuring the impact of skew on classification performance, as it does not magnify the differences between classifiers in the early retrieval range as effectively as Precision-Recall curves.
The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a measure used to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points.
It serves as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms, providing a single value that reflects overall classification quality.
a perfect classifier yields an AUC of 1, while an algorithm that performs random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5
The AUC is also described as the number of correctly ranked positive-negative pairs.
A key property of the AUC is that it is insensitive to class skew in the test set, distinguishing it from the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR), which varies with changing skew.

A higher AUC for one algorithm does not guarantee that it is strictly better than another, as this would require the ROC curve of the first algorithm to dominate the second across all operating points.
If the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess their relative quality using the AUC alone.

the AUC has been considered an incoherent measure of performance because it may use different scales when comparing different classifiers, although coherent interpretations have been proposed in the literature.
a classification threshold (cutoff) is a value chosen for a model
Different criteria can prefer different thresholds, meaning the selection is not unique but depends on the evaluation metric or objective used
The choice of this threshold has practical meaning in the application of the model

The threshold effect on precision, recall, and F1 describes how changing the score threshold of a classifier alters the set of predicted positives, thereby shifting the values of precision and recall.
A lower threshold results in more instances being predicted as positive.
As the score threshold increases, the number of predicted positives can stay the same or decrease.
At the lowest threshold, where every instance is labeled as positive, recall is 1, while precision equals the overall fraction of positives in the dataset.
As the threshold rises, precision may increase or decrease for the same value of recall, depending on the class of the instances added to or removed from the predicted positive set.
including a negative-class instance in the predicted positives drops precision without affecting recall, whereas including a positive-class instance can improve precision.
This dynamic causes the Precision-Recall (PR) curve to exhibit a zigzag pattern rather than being a smooth, monotonically increasing curve like the ROC curve.
The PR curve is sensitive to the skew factor, defined as the ratio of positives to the total number of instances (P / (P + N))
different PR curves are generated for different values of this skew factor.
Both precision and recall can be viewed as special cases of the Fβ measure by setting β=0 and β=∞, respectively.
The holdout method is a model evaluation technique in which the available dataset is split once into two parts: a training set and a test set.
The model is learned over the training set, and the resulting test error rate corresponds exactly to the performance of that specific model learned over that specific training set.

This distinguishes the holdout method from k-fold cross-validation, where a different model is learned at every run and the performance of every one of the k models on their respective test folds is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate.

In cross-validation, the computed error reflects the expected generalization error rate of the model selection approach when applied on a training set of the same size as one of the training folds, rather than the performance of a single model learned over a specific training set.
The holdout method can be repeated several times to obtain a distribution of the test error rates, an approach known as random subsampling or the repeated holdout method.
This repeated approach produces a distribution of the error rates that can be used to understand the variance of the test error rate.
Random subsampling is a model evaluation technique that repeats random hold-out splits several times and averages the resulting performance scores.
This approach is more stable than a single hold-out split, which suffers from high dependence on one specific division of the data.
Random subsampling does not guarantee that every instance is tested exactly once; some instances may be tested repeatedly while others may not be tested at all.
Random subsampling is related to simple random sampling, where there is an equal probability of selecting any particular object.

Sampling can be conducted with or without replacement; in sampling with replacement, objects are not removed from the population as they are selected, allowing the same object to be picked more than once.

This method is simpler to analyze because the probability of selecting any object remains constant during the sampling process, particularly when samples are relatively small compared to the data set size.
k-Fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that generalizes the holdout approach by segmenting the labeled data D (of size N) into k equal-sized partitions, or folds.
In each of the k runs, one partition is designated as the test set (D.test(i)) while the remaining k-1 partitions are used as the training set (D.train(i)).
This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set exactly once, ensuring that every data instance in D is used for both training and testing across the full procedure.
A different model is learned at every run, and the performance of each model on its respective test fold is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate.

This aggregated estimate reflects the expected generalization error rate of the model selection approach when applied to a training set of the same size as one of the training folds, rather than the performance of a single specific model learned over a fixed training set.
A small value of k results in smaller training sets for each run, which can lead to a larger estimate of generalization error rate than expected for a model trained on the entire labeled set.
Conversely, a high value of k results in larger training sets, reducing the bias in the estimate of generalization error rate.

For most practical applications, choosing k between 5 and 10 provides a reasonable approach for estimating generalization error rate, as each fold can utilize 80% to 90% of the labeled data for training.
An extreme case occurs when k equals N, known as the leave-one-out approach, where every run uses exactly one data instance for testing and the remainder for training.
While this utilizes as much data as possible for training, it can be computationally expensive for large datasets because the procedure must be repeated N times.
Standard k-fold cross validation produces a single estimate of the generalization error rate without providing information about the variance of that estimate.
To obtain variance information, one can run cross-validation for every possible partitioning of the data into k partitions, an approach known as complete cross-validation.
However, this is usually too expensive for large datasets.

A more practical solution is to repeat the cross-validation approach multiple times using different random partitionings of the data into k partitions at each iteration, and use the average test error rate as the estimate.
Additionally, standard k-fold cross validation does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data.
A solution to this issue is stratified cross-validation, which performs stratified sampling of positive and negative instances into the k partitions to preserve class distribution.
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is a special case of k-fold cross-validation where the number of folds k equals the total number of data instances N.
In this approach, the cross-validation procedure is repeated N times.
In each run, exactly one data instance is held out for testing, and the model is trained on the remaining N − 1 instances.
This configuration provides the maximum possible training data per run, which reduces the bias in the estimate of the generalization error rate compared to using a smaller number of folds.
LOOCV is computationally expensive for large data sets because the model must be trained and evaluated N times.
Additionally, because there is only one possible partitioning of the data for the leave-one-out approach, it is not possible to estimate the variance of the generalization error rate.

LOOCV is distinct from standard k-fold cross-validation (where k is typically between 5 and 10), stratified cross-validation (which preserves class proportions), and bootstrap sampling (which samples with replacement and tests on out-of-bag instances).

Bootstrap sampling is a statistical resampling technique in which data instances are randomly selected with replacement from an original data set to create a synthetic collection of the same size as the original.
Because the sampling is done with replacement, some instances may appear several times in the same training set, while others may be omitted.
On average, a bootstrap sample of size N contains approximately 63.2% of the unique instances from the original data, leaving about 36.8% of the instances unselected.
These unselected instances are known as out-of-bag instances and can be used as a test set for model evaluation.

The procedure is typically repeated multiple times to generate different training and test sets, allowing for the computation of distributions of performance measures such as accuracy, precision, and recall, or to estimate the distribution of the support of a frequent itemset.

In the context of ensemble methods like bagging (bootstrap aggregating), bootstrap sampling is used to train multiple classifiers on different subsets of the data, with the final prediction determined by majority voting.
The method is distinguished from k-fold cross-validation, which systematically splits data into subsets, and from hold-out methods, which split data once into training and test sets.

Stratified k-fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that extends standard k-fold cross validation by ensuring that each fold approximately preserves the class distribution of the full dataset.
In standard k-fold cross validation, the labeled data is segmented into k equal-sized partitions, or folds.
During each run, one partition is used for testing while the remaining partitions are used for training.
This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set once.

A key limitation of standard k-fold cross validation is that it does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data.
Stratified cross validation addresses this by performing a stratified sampling of the positive and negative instances into the k partitions.
This ensures that the proportion of class labels in every fold is kept the same as that of the overall data.
This approach is particularly useful for classification tasks where class imbalance might otherwise skew the evaluation results.
An empirical study by Kohavi suggests that ten-fold stratified cross validation is the best estimation method for performance metrics when compared to random subsampling and other k-fold variants.

The method is distinct from leave-one-out cross validation, which is a special case where k equals the total number of instances N, and from bootstrap sampling, which samples with replacement to form training sets and evaluates on out-of-bag instances.
Feature selection is a process that chooses an optimal subset of features according to a certain criterion.

It is an effective form of dealing with dimensionality reduction, which constitutes a serious obstacle to the competence of most learning algorithms, especially due to the fact that they usually are computationally expensive.
The goal of feature selection is to remove redundant and irrelevant features, reduce acquisition and computational cost, improve model quality, reduce model complexity, and improve efficiency.
Conceptually, feature subset selection is a search over all possible subsets of features.
Many different types of search strategies can be used, but the search strategy should be computationally inexpensive and should find optimal or near optimal sets of features.
It is usually not possible to satisfy both requirements, and thus, trade-offs are necessary.

The feature selection process is viewed as consisting of four parts: a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of a new subset of features, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure.
There are three standard approaches to feature selection: embedded, filter, and wrapper.
Filter methods and wrapper methods differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features.
In feature evaluation, the common procedure is to measure the correlation between any feature with the class.
Denoting by R(A) a dependence measure between feature A and class C, we choose feature Ai over feature Aj if R(Ai) > R(Aj).
If A and C are statistically independent, they are not correlated and removing A should not affect the class separability regarding the rest of the features.
In a contrary case, the feature should be selected because it could somewhat explain the trend of the class.
One of the most used dependence measures is the Pearson correlation coefficient, which measures the degree of linear correlation between two variables.

Feature selection keeps original features, whereas dimensionality reduction is often reserved for those techniques that reduce the dimensionality of a data set by creating new attributes that are a combination of the old attributes.
The reduction of dimensionality by selecting attributes that are a subset of the old is known as feature subset selection or feature selection.

While some irrelevant and redundant attributes can be eliminated immediately by using common sense or domain knowledge, selecting the best subset of features frequently requires a systematic approach.
Unfortunately, since the number of subsets involving n attributes is 2^n, such an approach is impractical in most situations and alternative strategies are needed.
In clustering, the coordinates were features.
In decision trees, split attributes were features.
In Naive Bayes, probability variables were features.
Feature selection now asks whether all those features are actually needed.
Accuracy-based feature selection needs a target label, so it belongs to supervised learning.
In clustering, there is no target label, so accuracy is not available unless external labels are provided.
For clustering, replace accuracy by an internal cluster validity measure such as silhouette, SSE, cohesion, or separation.
A random forest is induced by building many decision trees.
For each tree, a bootstrap sample of the training data is drawn by sampling instances with replacement.

The tree is then grown using random feature selection at each split: instead of considering all attributes, only a random subset of attributes is considered, and the best split among that subset is chosen.
For classification, the final random-forest prediction is obtained by majority voting over the trees.
The main random components are therefore the bootstrap sampling of training instances and the random selection of candidate attributes at each split.
Redundant features are attributes that duplicate much or all of the information contained in one or more other attributes.
A common example is the purchase price of a product and the amount of sales tax paid, which contain much of the same information.
In the context of feature selection, the objective is to identify important features and discard others as redundant or irrelevant.
Redundant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of clusters found, and in probability models like Naive Bayes, they can cause similar evidence to be counted twice.
Inter-feature redundancy is typically assessed by measuring association or correlation between pairs of selected features.
The choice of measure depends on the data type: Pearson correlation is used for numerical features, Spearman correlation for ordinal features, and the chi-square test for categorical features.
If two input features are strongly related or associated, one may be redundant.
However, removal decisions should also consider cost, missingness, interpretability, and performance.
Consistency measures offer another approach by aiming to find a minimum number of features that separate classes as well as the full set, defined by the condition P(C|FullSet) = P(C|SubSet).
P(C|FullSet) = P(C|SubSet)
An inconsistency occurs when two examples have the same feature values but different class labels.
Using consistency measures allows for the removal of both irrelevant and redundant features.
Decision trees can also handle redundant attributes because redundant attributes show similar gains in purity, leading the algorithm to select only one of them as a split condition.
An attribute is defined as irrelevant if it is not useful for the classification task.
irrelevant attributes are poorly associated with the target class labels
irrelevant attributes provide little or no gain in purity
irrelevant attributes are typically passed over by other more relevant features
the presence of a small number of irrelevant attributes will not impact the decision tree construction process

if the classification problem is complex, such as involving interactions among attributes, and there are a large number of irrelevant attributes, some of these attributes may be accidentally chosen during the tree-growing process
students' ID numbers are irrelevant to the task of predicting students' grade point averages
Redundant and irrelevant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of the clusters that are found
Feature selection techniques can help to improve the accuracy of decision trees by eliminating the irrelevant attributes during preprocessing
in minimum subset techniques, an algorithm returns a minimum feature subset and no difference is made for features in the subset; whatever is relevant within the subset is otherwise irrelevant
in search directions where the feature set shrinks and the subset grows, the subset may store only the irrelevant features
The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon where data analysis becomes significantly harder as the dimensionality of the data increases.
Dimensionality is defined as the number of attributes that the objects in a data set possess.
As the number of dimensions increases, the data space grows very quickly, causing the data to become increasingly sparse in the space it occupies.

distances between points become less discriminative, making nearest and farthest points less clearly separated; differences in density become less meaningful; and local neighborhoods may become nearly empty unless the radius parameter is set very large, which can cause neighborhoods to stop being locally meaningful.
For clustering algorithms, these effects are critical because they rely on density and distance relationships.
Consequently, many clustering and classification algorithms have trouble with high-dimensional data, leading to reduced classification accuracy and poor quality clusters.

The curse of dimensionality is a primary motivation for dimensionality reduction in data preprocessing, which aims to eliminate irrelevant features and reduce noise to make models more understandable and easier to visualize.
some methods, such as kernel functions in support vector machines, can represent nonlinear decision boundaries without suffering from the curse of dimensionality
The Filter Approach is one of three standard approaches to feature selection, alongside embedded and wrapper methods.
It operates independently of the data mining method subsequently employed, a property that distinguishes it from wrapper approaches which are typically coupled to a specific learner.
The name 'filter' derives from the process of filtering undesirable features out before the learning phase begins.

Within a common feature selection architecture, filter methods share components such as a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure; however, they differ from wrapper methods specifically in the way they evaluate a subset of features.
Because the filter approach is independent of the downstream model, filter methods are usually faster than their wrapper counterparts.

While the literature also recommends filtering for the detection and treatment of noisy data, the Filter Approach in the context of feature selection is defined by its pre-learning feature evaluation and selection mechanism.
In the context of feature selection, some authors differentiate a sub-category from filtering called rankers.
This unit is positioned within the broader filter model, which operates independently of the data mining method subsequently employed.
The name 'filter' proceeds from filtering the undesirable features out before learning.
The reasons that influence the use of filters are those related to noise removal, data simplification, and increasing the performance of any data mining technique.
The wrapper approach is a feature selection strategy that uses a learning algorithm as a black box to evaluate feature subsets, aiming to improve the predictive performance of that specific learner.

Unlike filter methods, which cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, wrapper methods are designed to select features that accomplish the highest predictive accuracy for a fixed learning algorithm.

The process typically involves two stages: first, feature subset selection where the best subset is chosen using the accuracy provided by the learning algorithm on training data as the criterion; and second, re-learning the data mining model with the best subset.
To avoid overfitting, the wrapper approach employs statistical validation, such as cross-validation, to agree on a predictive measure.

While wrapper approaches are an interesting choice in some domains, they require higher computational costs and are usually slower than filter methods, which can be a crucial factor under time constraints.
Experimental studies have shown that results vary among learners, often recommending wrapper approaches for each kind of learner to optimize performance.

The filter versus wrapper trade-off in feature selection concerns the choice between two distinct evaluation strategies: filters evaluate features before learning, whereas wrappers evaluate subsets by using the learner.

Both approaches can be encompassed within a common architecture that includes a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of a new subset of features, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure; filter methods and wrapper methods differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features.

A wrapper model consists of two stages: (1) feature subset selection, which selects the best subset using the accuracy provided by the learning algorithm (on training data) as a criterion; and (2) a stage that is the same as in the filter model.
Since only the best subset is kept in stage 1, the data mining model must be learned again with the best subset.
Wrapper models can achieve the purpose of improving the particular learner's predictive performance.
The trade-off is that filter models cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, whereas wrapper methods do.
However, wrapper methods are usually slower than filters, and it may be crucial to determine the best feature selection choice under time constraints.
In such cases, filters are thought to be more appropriate than wrapper-based feature selectors.
Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) is a feature selection algorithm that operates by iteratively expanding a candidate set.
The process begins with an empty set of features, denoted as S.
As the search progresses, features are added into S one at a time according to a criterion that distinguishes the best feature from the others.
This expansion continues until the set S reaches the full set of original features or until a specific stopping condition is met.
The stopping criteria for SFG can be defined as a threshold for the number of relevant features, m, or as the generation of all possible subsets in a brute force mode.
SFG is classified as a heuristic method, and it is used to select the next best feature until the selected set satisfies the defined criterion.
Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a heuristic feature selection method that starts with the full set of features and iteratively removes features one at a time.
The algorithm is defined by the function SBG(F, U), where F is the full set of features and U is the measure or criterion used to evaluate subsets.
The procedure initializes a set S to hold the removed features.

In a repeat loop, the algorithm selects the next feature to remove using f = GetNext(F) (or f = FindNextWorst(F, U) in the heuristic variant), removes it from the current set via F = F  setminus {f}, and adds it to the removed set via S = S cup {f}.
The loop continues until the remaining set F fails to satisfy the criterion U or until F becomes empty.
When the stopping condition is met, the algorithm returns F cup {f}, where f is the last removed feature.
This return value is justified because f was the last feature removed, and after removing it, the remaining set failed the criterion.

SBG is distinguished from Sequential Forward Generation (SFG), which starts from an empty set and adds features, and from Bidirectional Generation (BG), which combines forward and backward search directions.
SBG is a heuristic method because it uses greedy choices to select the next worst feature to remove.

Bidirectional Generation (BG) is a feature set generation algorithm that begins the search in both directions, performing Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) and Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) concurrently.
This approach takes advantage of both SFG and SBG by combining forward and backward search.

The search terminates under one of two conditions: (1) when one search finds the best subset comprised of m features before it reaches the exact middle, or (2) when both searches achieve the middle of the search space.
The bidirectional generation is shown in operation in the algorithm.
Random Generation (RG) is a feature set generation algorithm that produces subsets of features at random.
It starts the search in a random direction, and the choice of adding or removing a feature is a random decision.
RG tries to avoid stagnation into a local optima by not following a fixed way for subset generation.
Unlike Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) or Sequential Backward Generation (SBG), the size of the subset of features cannot be stipulated.

A random generation scheme is based on a good random number generator attached with a function called RandGen(F) in such a way that every combination of features F has a chance to occur and only once.
S = RandGen(F)
RG generates random subsets and returns the best satisfactory subset found when the stopping criterion is reached.
RG is non-deterministic because the generated subsets are random.
Exhaustive search is a feature selection strategy that explores the entire search space to identify the optimal subset of features.
It is defined by its completeness: it covers all possible combinations of features, distinguishing it from heuristic or non-deterministic approaches that may prune the search space.
The method can be implemented in two primary directions: forward search, which grows the feature subset gradually, and backward search, which reduces the subset by removing features one at a time.
In backward search, the process starts with the full set of features and iteratively removes features to find the optimal subset.
The space complexity of exhaustive search is O(2^M), where M is the total number of features.

If a threshold m is established for the minimum number of features to be selected, the search space is defined by the sum of combinations from 0 to m, independent of whether the search is forward or backward.
Exhaustive search is the only method that guarantees the optimality of the selected feature subset.
However, because of its high computational cost, it is often impractical for large datasets.
In such cases, exact algorithms like backtracking and branch and bound can be used to find an optimal subset without visiting all possible states.

Exhaustive search is typically paired with evaluation measures such as probability, consistency, or accuracy, and it is considered a 'complete' search strategy in the taxonomy of feature selection methods.
Heuristic search is a feature selection strategy that employs heuristics to carry out the search, preventing brute force exploration while ensuring the discovery of a non-optimal subset of features.

It is positioned as a middle ground between exhaustive search, which guarantees optimality but is impractical for high-dimensional data, and nondeterministic search, which improves quality over time without a defined stopping point.
The search process draws a path connecting the beginning and the end in a manner similar to depth-first search, where the maximum length of this path is M and the number of subsets generated is O(M).
The choice of the heuristic is crucial to finding a subset closer to the optimal one in a faster operation.
In the categorization of feature selection methods, heuristic search is one of the three values for the Search Strategy dimension, alongside Complete and Nondeterministic.
It can be combined with different search directions, such as forward or backward, and evaluation measures.

One specific implementation mentioned is the Mutual Information based Feature Selection (MIFS), which uses a greedy algorithm to replace impossible exhaustive search by choosing the next feature that maximizes information about the class relative to the average mutual information with already selected features.
Non-Deterministic Search is a feature selection strategy also known as random search.
It is characterized by the random choice of search direction, meaning the algorithm does not pursue a fixed path or specific direction for subset generation.
This approach is non-deterministic because the generated subsets are random, which allows the method to avoid stagnation in local optima.
A key property of this strategy is that it can generate best subsets constantly and keep improving the quality of selected features as time goes by.

There are two specific properties associated with this type of search: first, it is unnecessary to wait until the search ends to obtain results, and second, while the optimal set is not known to be obtained at a specific moment, the algorithm knows which subset is better than the previous one and which one is the best at the moment.
In the categorization of feature selection methods, Non-Deterministic Search is one of the values for the Search strategy dimension, alongside Complete and Heuristic search.
It is typically paired with a Random search direction, as combinations of non-deterministic search with forward or backward generation of features are considered impractical.
The chi-squared test is a statistical method used to evaluate the independence of categorical or nominal attributes, particularly when the set of values is finite.
It is commonly applied in feature selection to identify redundant attributes or to select interdependent variables at a presumed significant level.
The basic procedure involves computing the expected value of every entry in a contingency table under the null hypothesis that the items are statistically independent.
The differences between the observed and expected values are then used to compute a test statistic that follows the chi-squared distribution.
This statistic is compared against a tabulated chi-squared value using the suitable degrees of freedom, which is often (q - 1) where q represents the number of outcomes.
If the computed statistic exceeds the tabulated value, the null hypothesis is rejected, indicating that the attributes are statistically correlated.
The test is specifically suited for categorical features and is used to check whether two categorical attributes are independent.
The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient is a dependence measure used to quantify the degree of linear correlation between two numerical variables.
It is described as the most well-known correlation coefficient and is specifically applied to numerical features to assess linear relationships.
The coefficient is calculated using the values of the two attributes, their respective means, and their standard deviations.

For two variables A and B, the correlation coefficient r_{A,B} is given by the formula: r_{A,B} = (Σ_{i=1}^{m} (a_i - A̅)(b_i - B̅)) / (m σ_A σ_B), which is equivalent to (Σ_{i=1}^{m} (a_i b_i) - m A̅ B̅) / (m σ_A σ_B).

In this expression, m represents the number of instances, a_i and b_i are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A̅ and B̅ are the mean values of A and B respectively, and σ_A and σ_B are the standard deviations of A and B.

An alternative formulation for variables X and Y is ρ(X,Y) = Σ_i (x_i - x̄)(y_i - ȳ) / [ (Σ_i (x_i - x̄)^2) (Σ_i (y_i - ȳ)^2) ]^{1/2}, where x_i and y_i are the measurements and x̄ and ȳ are the means.
This measure is distinct from rank-based or categorical measures, as it specifically targets linear association in numeric data.
Covariance is a statistical measure used to determine how much two variables change together.
It is defined as the expected value of the product of the deviations of two attributes from their respective means.
Cov(A, B) = E((A - A̅)(B - B̅)) = (1/m) * Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ (aᵢ - A̅)(bᵢ - B̅)

In this expression, m represents the number of instances, aᵢ and bᵢ are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A̅ and B̅ are the mean values of A and B respectively, and E(A) and E(B) denote the expected values of the attributes.
The sign of the covariance indicates the direction of the relationship between the variables.
If two attributes vary similarly, such that when A is greater than its mean A̅, B is also likely to be greater than its mean B̅, the covariance is positive.
Conversely, if one attribute tends to be above its expected value while the other is below its expected value, the covariance is negative.
When the two variables are independent, the expected value of their product equals the product of their expected values (E(A·B) = E(A)·E(B)), which results in a covariance of zero.
However, a covariance of zero does not necessarily imply that the attributes are independent, as some random variables may have a covariance of zero while still being dependent.
Additional assumptions, such as the data following multivariate normal distributions, are necessary to determine independence from a zero covariance.
Covariance is closely related to the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient.

The correlation coefficient r(A,B) is calculated by dividing the covariance of A and B by the product of their standard deviations: r(A,B) = Cov(A, B) / (σA * σB), where σA and σB are the standard deviations of A and B.
This relationship allows covariance to be used in assessing redundancy between numerical attributes, as high correlation (derived from covariance) may indicate that one attribute can be removed.
Spearman Rank Correlation is a measure of association defined as the Pearson correlation computed on the ranks of the variables.
r_s = ρ(R(X), R(Y))
r_s denotes the Spearman correlation coefficient, ρ represents the Pearson correlation function, and R(X) and R(Y) represent the ranks of variables X and Y
This measure is specifically used for ordinal variables, ranked variables, or numerical variables where a monotonic relationship is more important than a linear relationship.

In contrast to Pearson correlation, which measures linear relationships between numerical variables, Spearman correlation measures monotonic relationships by applying the Pearson calculation to ranks.
The resulting value falls within the range [−1, 1], with a value of 0 indicating no monotonic relationship.

When calculating Spearman correlation in the presence of tied values, the procedure requires using average ranks and computing the Pearson correlation on those ranks, rather than using a shortcut formula.
Information Gain (Feature Goodness) is a criterion used in feature selection to evaluate how well a feature reduces uncertainty in a dataset.

In the context of predictive learning, the 'message' is the output feature or class in classification, and an information measure U is defined such that larger values represent higher levels of uncertainty.
The information gain from a feature A, denoted as IG(A), is defined as the difference between the prior uncertainty and the expected posterior uncertainty using A.

In this formula, I(D) represents the information for the dataset D, D_j is the j-th child subset produced after splitting D using attribute A, |D_j|/|D| is the weight of child node j, and I(D_j^A) is the information for D_j due to partitioning D at A.
A feature evaluation model inferred from this concept states that feature Ai is chosen instead of feature Aj if IG(Ai) > IG(Aj), meaning Ai reduces more uncertainty than Aj.
This idea is used in algorithms like C4.5 for selecting a feature to generate new branches.

However, Information Gain is biased toward attributes with many distinct values; for example, if an attribute has a unique value for each instance (such as an ID), a multiway split can create one pure child node per instance, resulting in zero weighted child entropy and maximal Information Gain.
Shannon entropy is a commonly used uncertainty function that serves as the standard measure for quantifying uncertainty in classification contexts.
It is frequently employed to define information gain, which motivates the concept as a measure of uncertainty reduction.
The mathematical formulation for entropy is given by the formula: Entropy = −∑(i=0 to c−1) p_i(t) log_2 p_i(t), where p_i(t) represents the probability of class i at time t.
In specific applications, such as a binary classification problem with equal class distributions, the entropy value can reach 1, indicating maximal uncertainty.
For instance, a calculation for a parent node with 10 positive and 10 negative instances yields an entropy of 1, demonstrating the measure's behavior in balanced datasets.

Shannon entropy is distinct from information gain, which uses entropy to evaluate the reduction in uncertainty after a split, and from gain ratio, which adjusts for the number of distinct values in an attribute to mitigate bias toward high-cardinality features.
The null hypothesis (H0) is a formal statement in statistical testing that serves as the baseline assumption to be evaluated against observed data.
It is explicitly defined alongside an alternative hypothesis (H1) to provide a rigorous framework for assessing whether an observed result is statistically significant.

The null hypothesis represents the distribution of a test statistic under the assumption that no effect or difference exists; for example, in anomaly detection, H0 states that an instance belongs to the normal class, while in classifier evaluation, it states that the classifier has not learned a generalizable relationship between attributes and class labels.
The primary role of the null hypothesis is to enable the calculation of a p-value, which is the probability of falsely rejecting H0 when it is actually true.
This allows for a more objective assessment of evidence compared to significance testing alone, which does not explicitly specify an alternative hypothesis.

A critical distinction is that failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to 'accepting' it; a non-significant result may still arise from the alternative distribution or a misspecified null model.
Consequently, the null hypothesis provides the reference distribution against which the extremity of a test statistic is measured to determine if it falls within a critical region.
A test statistic, typically denoted R, is a numerical quantity used to quantify the evidence in an observed outcome with respect to a null hypothesis.
It typically summarizes every possible outcome as a single count or real-valued value, enabling the computation of the probability of an outcome under the null hypothesis.

The test statistic measures how 'extreme' an observed result is under the null hypothesis; for example, in a stockbroker problem, R could be the number of successful decisions made in a fixed number of trials, reducing a complex outcome to a single count.
The definition of 'extreme' depends on the choice of the null hypothesis and the design of the test statistic.

An observed test statistic can be considered extreme if it is greater than or equal to a certain value (right-tailed), smaller than or equal to a certain value (left-tailed), or outside a specified interval (two-sided).
These cases correspond to one-sided and two-sided tests, respectively.
In hypothesis testing, the test statistic is chosen to differentiate the behavior of results under the null hypothesis from the behavior of results under the alternative hypothesis.
The distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis (the null distribution) and, sometimes, under the alternative hypothesis must be modeled.

Given these distributions, the framework of hypothesis testing decides whether to reject or not reject the null hypothesis based on the evidence provided by the test statistic computed from an observed result.
This decision is typically made by specifying a critical region—a range of possible values of the test statistic that are too extreme under the null hypothesis.
If the observed test statistic falls in this region, the null hypothesis is rejected; otherwise, it is not rejected.
The p-value of an observed test statistic is the probability of obtaining that value or something more extreme from the null distribution.
P-values capture the aggregate tail probabilities of the null distribution for test statistic values that are at least as extreme as the observed value.
The reason for accounting for 'something more extreme' is that the probability of any particular result is often 0 or close to 0.
The test statistic is used in various contexts, including cluster analysis, anomaly detection, and association analysis.

In cluster analysis, the test statistic is typically a cluster validity measure (e.g., SSE or silhouette coefficient) used to test whether the observed clustering is significant compared to random partitioning.
In anomaly detection, the anomaly score of an instance serves as the test statistic, with the null hypothesis that the instance belongs to the normal class.

In association analysis, the test statistic measures the deviation of an observed contingency table from the null hypothesis of no association among items; for example, the chi-squared test statistic is computed from the differences between observed and expected values in a contingency table.
A primary requirement for conducting statistical testing is knowing how the test statistic is distributed under the null hypothesis.

This distribution can be estimated by fitting statistical models (e.g., normal or binomial) to test statistic values from data sets generated under the null hypothesis, or by using non-parametric approaches such as counting the fraction of times the test statistic generated under the null distribution exceeds the observed value.
When the distribution of the test statistic depends on the number of samples, increasing the sample size helps obtain less variable estimates of the true null and alternative distributions.
The minimum number of samples required for ensuring a low value of the significance level while having high power is often determined by power analysis.
The significance level, denoted by α, is a fixed threshold on p-values that is decided before any tests are performed.

A result is called statistically significant if its p-value is lower than this threshold, which provides sufficient evidence to believe the observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis and convinces us to reject it.
While every result has a different p-value, the significance level remains a constant for the testing process.
Common choices for this level include 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%).
The p-value of a statistically significant result denotes the probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true.

Rejecting the null hypothesis if the test statistic falls in the critical region is equivalent to evaluating the p-value and rejecting the null hypothesis if the p-value falls below the pre-specified threshold.
In the context of multiple hypothesis testing, the significance level can be adjusted to balance power and false positives.
In the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, the significance level for the i-th p-value is computed as αi = i × α/m.
This approach strikes a balance between the overly conservative Bonferroni procedure and the overly liberal naïve approach, resulting in higher power without producing too many false positives.

The BH procedure declares the first k p-values as significant, where k is the largest index such that the p-value is lower than its significance level, guaranteeing that the False Discovery Rate (FDR) is smaller than α.
One-sided and two-sided tests are distinct approaches to statistical hypothesis testing that differ in how the probability of the null distribution is allocated across its tails.
A one-sided test, which can be right-tailed or left-tailed, concentrates the entire probability of the significance level (such as 0.05) into a single tail of the distribution.
A two-sided test splits this probability equally between both tails, resulting in 0.025 probability in each tail when the significance level is 0.05.

The choice between these tests depends on the specific research question: a one-sided test is used when the hypothesis is directional, such as testing whether one entity is better than another, while a two-sided test is used when the hypothesis is non-directional, asking whether two entities are different in either direction.

A low p-value in either type of test indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution, providing sufficient evidence to believe that the observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis and justifying its rejection.
In the context of classifier comparison, a two-tailed test typically uses a threshold such as |Z| > 1.96 at a significance level of 0.05 to determine if classifiers are significantly different.
Hunt's algorithm is a generic procedure used for growing decision trees in a greedy fashion.
It serves as the basis for several current decision tree classifier implementations, including CART, C4.5, and ID3.
The algorithm grows the decision tree recursively.
It begins with a single root node that is associated with all training instances.
The tree is grown in a top-down fashion by making a series of locally optimal decisions regarding which attribute to use when partitioning the training data.
During the process, training instances are propagated to child nodes based on attribute values.
If a node contains training instances from only one class label, it becomes a leaf node.
If a node contains instances from more than one class, it can be further expanded.

In cases where a child node is created but no training instances possess the required attribute values, the node is empty; one method to handle this is to declare the empty node as a leaf node using the class label that occurs most frequently among the training instances associated with its parent node.
Node impurity is a measure of how dissimilar the class labels are for the data instances belonging to a common node.
It is used to identify the best attribute test condition for a node by evaluating the impurity of a single node and the collective impurity of its child nodes.
Common impurity measures include entropy, the Gini index, and error rate.
These measures are consistent in that if a node has lower entropy than another node, its Gini index and error rate will also be lower.

All three measures yield a zero impurity value if a node contains instances from only a single class, and reach maximum impurity if the node contains equal proportions of instances from multiple classes.

Maximizing this gain is equivalent to minimizing the weighted impurity measure of the children, as I(parent) remains constant for all candidate attribute test conditions.
When entropy is used, the resulting difference is known as information gain, and I(parent) ≥ I(children).
A limitation of impurity measures like entropy and the Gini index is their tendency to favor qualitative attributes with a large number of distinct values.

Consequently, a low impurity value alone is insufficient to determine a good attribute test condition, as the number of children produced by the splitting attribute must also be considered to avoid increasing model complexity and susceptibility to overfitting.
The misclassification rate, also referred to as the error rate, represents the fraction of instances that are misclassified.

In the context of a decision tree node, the majority-class error rate is calculated as the proportion of instances not belonging to the majority class; for example, a node containing 9 negative and 1 positive instances has a majority-class error rate of 1/10, or 0.1.
Misclassification rate is used as an impurity measure to evaluate attribute test conditions and determine the best split between values.
It is distinct from entropy, which is a more general impurity measure rather than just a fraction of misclassified instances.

Gain Ratio is a metric used in decision tree construction to select attributes for splitting.

Gain Ratio is used to correct a bias in Information Gain, which tends to prefer attributes with many distinct values (high-cardinality attributes), such as an ID.

Splitting continuous attributes is a key step in the decision tree process that involves partitioning the possible values of a continuous attribute into a number of contiguous intervals.
This process is often handled via discretization, which groups adjacent values into a finite number of intervals.
Discretization can be performed using several techniques: equal interval width, equal frequency, entropy-based, or clustering.
For the purpose of creating a split, the attribute test condition can be expressed in two primary ways:
A binary split: This uses a comparison test.

Any value between the minimum and maximum attribute values in the training data can be used for the test, though it is sufficient to consider only the distinct attribute values in the training set as candidate split positions.
A multiway split: This uses a range query.
This requires a collection of attribute value ranges that are mutually exclusive and cover the entire range between the minimum and maximum values observed in the training set.
Following discretization, a new ordinal value is assigned to each interval, and the attribute test condition is then defined using this newly constructed ordinal attribute.
Prior probability, denoted as $P(y)$, represents the probability of a class $y$ before observing any attribute values.
It captures prior beliefs about the distribution of class labels independent of observed attribute values, reflecting how common each class is before seeing a new instance.
In the context of Naive Bayes, the prior probability is a component used to compute the posterior probability of each class.
In extreme cases where no attributes are observed for a data instance, the prior probability $P(y)$ can be used as an estimate of the posterior probability.
The prior probability can be obtained through two primary methods: 1. Using expert knowledge. 2. Inferring it from the historical distribution of class labels.
Specifically, it can be estimated from a training set by computing the fraction of training instances that belong to each class.
The Naive Independence Assumption is the core premise of the Naive Bayes classifier, stating that attributes are conditionally independent given the class.
This means the joint conditional probability of attributes given a class Y can be factored as the product of the conditional probabilities of those attributes considered separately.
This assumption is described as 'naive' because it assumes conditional independence given the class rather than unconditional independence.

While this assumption may seem too rigid or unrealistic—particularly in classification problems where attributes remain dependent even after conditioning on the class labels—the method has worked surprisingly well for applications such as text classification.

In terms of Bayesian networks, the Naive Bayes classifier is a special type of network where the target class Y is the root of a tree and every attribute is connected to that root node by a directed edge.
This structure is more restrictive than general Bayesian networks, which can express a richer class of conditional independence statements.
A primary limit of this assumption is that correlated attributes can degrade the performance of the classifier because the assumption of conditional independence no longer holds for such attributes.
The NB Learning Phase is the training phase where parameters for the prior probability $P(y)$ and the class-conditional probabilities $P(x|y)$ are learned.
The prior probability $P(y)$ is estimated from the training set by calculating the fraction of training instances that belong to each class.
To compute the class-conditional probabilities, one approach is to determine the fraction of training instances of a given class for every possible combination of attribute values.
The zero-frequency problem occurs when an unobserved class-attribute combination receives a probability of zero.
This typically happens when the training set is small and certain class-attribute combinations are simply never observed.
If the conditional probability of any attribute value given a class is zero, the entire class-conditional product becomes zero, effectively wiping out the product for that class.
