Model overfitting is a phenomenon that occurs when an overly complex model is selected in the pursuit of minimizing the training error rate.

Such a model captures specific patterns in the training data but fails to learn the true nature of the relationships between attributes and class labels in the overall data, leading to poor generalization performance on an independently chosen test set.
Overfitting is often regarded as being caused by the presence of noise, though it can also be viewed as an artifact of a failure to compensate for the multiple comparisons problem.
In Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), overfitting may occur if the number of redundant or irrelevant attributes is large.
In the context of decision trees, an overfitted model is characterized by complicated decision boundaries.

For example, a complex tree may create narrow regions in the input space to cover only one or two training instances; because these regions are mostly dominated by opposite-class instances in the overall data, the model is fine-tuning itself to patterns specific to the training set rather than generalizable rules.

To avoid overfitting, model selection should consider both the training error rate and model complexity, a strategy inspired by Occam's razor (the principle of parsimony), which prefers the simpler model when two models have the same errors.
Additionally, to ensure the absence of overfitting, the test set used to estimate the generalization error rate should be independently chosen and never examined during the model selection process.

The optimistic error estimate, also known as the resubstitution estimate, is an approach for estimating the generalization error rate of a decision tree by simply using the training error rate of that tree.

This estimate is considered optimistic because if a classifier is trained and tested on the same data, the performance estimate is usually too optimistic; the classifier may memorize training examples and still perform poorly on unseen instances.
In the context of comparing decision trees, the optimistic error estimate prefers the tree with the lower training error.
The pessimistic error estimate is an approach used to model the generalization performance of a decision tree on unseen test instances.
It is termed pessimistic because it assumes the generalization error rate will be worse than the training error rate by adding a penalty term for model complexity.
The estimate is calculated as the training error of the decision tree plus a complexity penalty.

In this context, a hyper-parameter Ω is used to make a trade-off between reducing training error and minimizing model complexity; Ω can be viewed as the relative cost of adding a leaf node compared to incurring a training error.
The value of Ω can be selected using a validation set.
In the process of rule pruning, classification rules are extracted for every path from the root to a leaf node.
A simplified rule is created by removing one of the conjuncts.
The simplified rule with the lowest pessimistic error rate is retained, provided its error rate is lower than that of the original rule.
This pruning step is repeated until the pessimistic error of the rule cannot be improved further, after which duplicate rules are discarded.
Reduced error pruning is a pruning method used to avoid overfitting in decision trees.
It is characterized by keeping a prune only if the validation performance is no worse than it was before the prune.
The reduced-error-pruning estimate is defined as the validation-set error rate.
The ground truth for this process is the Class column in the validation set; the tree's predictions are compared against these validation labels.
To implement this approach, the generalization error rate of the tree is computed using a validation set.
In the context of rule pruning, a metric monotonically related to the rule's accuracy on the validation set is computed to determine if pruning is needed.
Pruning is performed starting from the last conjunct added to the rule; if the metric improves after pruning, the conjunct is removed.
Reduced error estimates can be formally ambiguous unless a tie rule is assumed.
For example, a tie at a specific node (e.g., A = 0) may be resolved as either positive (+) or negative (-), which can determine whether a specific tree is selected or if a prune is accepted.

The training set and test set split is a method of partitioning a labeled data set into two disjoint sets to facilitate model development and evaluation.
The most basic technique for this is the holdout method, where a labeled set D is randomly partitioned into a training set (D.train) and a test set (D.test).
The procedure for the holdout method involves splitting the available data once.
A classification model is induced from the training data, and its error rate on the test data is then used as an estimate of the generalization error rate.

The proportion of data reserved for each set is typically at the discretion of the analysts; for example, common splits include two-thirds for training and one-third for testing, or 10% for training and 90% for testing.
This method is used to evaluate how well patterns learned in the training set generalize over the test set.
A primary limit of the holdout method is that its estimate can have high variance because it depends on a single random split, making it split-dependent.
A sample is considered representative if it possesses approximately the same property of interest as the original data set from which it was drawn.
if the mean (average) of the data objects is the property of interest, a representative sample is one with a mean close to that of the original data.
The key principle for effective sampling is that using a representative sample will work almost as well as using the entire data set.

Because sampling is a statistical process, the representativeness of any specific sample varies; therefore, the objective is to select a sampling scheme that ensures a high probability of obtaining a representative sample.
The target attribute is the specific variable that a model is designed to predict or characterize.
In classification tasks, this is referred to as the target class label, and attributes that are poorly associated with these target class labels are considered irrelevant.
In regression problems, the target attribute is a continuous variable.
In the context of quantitative association rules, the target attribute is a continuous variable denoted as t.

For a frequent itemset A, the average value of t among transactions covered by A is represented by $mu$, while the average value of t among transactions not covered by A is denoted by $mu ^ {  prime }$.
To generate statistics-based quantitative association rules, the target attribute used to characterize interesting population segments must be specified.

The process involves: 1. Withholding the target attribute from the data. 2. Binarizing the remaining categorical and continuous attributes. 3. Applying algorithms such as FP-growth or Apriori to extract frequent itemsets from the binarized data to identify interesting population segments. 4. Summarizing the distribution of the target attribute within each segment using descriptive statistics, such as variance, mean, absolute deviation, or median.
Attributes are classified into four primary types: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio.

These types are cumulative, meaning each attribute type possesses all the properties and operations of the types above it; for example, any property or operation valid for nominal, ordinal, and interval attributes is also valid for ratio attributes.
However, statistical operations appropriate for one type are not necessarily appropriate for those above it.
Attributes are broadly grouped into two categories: categorical (qualitative) and quantitative (numeric).
Categorical attributes consist of nominal and ordinal types and generally lack most properties of numbers.
Quantitative attributes consist of interval and ratio types, are represented by numbers, and possess most properties of numbers; these can be either integer-valued or continuous.
In terms of value counts, nominal and ordinal attributes are typically binary or discrete, while interval and ratio attributes are typically continuous.
Notably, count attributes are discrete but are classified as ratio attributes.
When representing attributes in a neural network's input layer, numerical or binary attributes are typically represented by a single node.
Categorical attributes are represented either by a different node for each categorical value or by encoding the k-ary attribute using input nodes.

To binarize a categorical attribute with m values, the following procedure is used: 1. Uniquely assign each original value to an integer in the interval [0, m-1]. If the attribute is ordinal, the assignment must maintain the original order. 2. Convert these m integers to binary. Since n = [log2(m)] binary digits are required to represent these integers, represent them using n binary attributes.
A cluster is generally defined as a set of objects that share some property.
Because the definition of a cluster is imprecise, the best definition depends on the desired results and the nature of the data.
Idealistic/Well-Separated: A cluster is a set of objects where each object is closer (or more similar) to every other object in the cluster than to any object not in the cluster.
Sometimes a threshold is used to require that all objects in a cluster be sufficiently close or similar.
This definition is satisfied only when natural clusters are quite far from each other; such clusters can have any shape and do not need to be globular.
Prototype-based (Center-based): A cluster is a set of objects where each object is closer (or more similar) to the prototype that defines the cluster than to the prototype of any other cluster.

The prototype is often a centroid (the average/mean of all points) for continuous attributes, or a medoid (the most representative point) when centroids are not meaningful, such as with categorical attributes.
These clusters tend to be globular.
Density-based: A cluster is a dense region of objects surrounded by a region of low density.
This definition is often used when noise and outliers are present, or when clusters are intertwined or irregular.

Graph-based: If data is represented as a graph (nodes as objects, links as connections), a cluster is a connected component—a group of objects connected to one another but having no connection to objects outside the group.
A specific example is a contiguity-based cluster, where objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance of each other.
This is useful for irregular or intertwined clusters, though noise can create bridges that merge distinct clusters.

Clusters are described differently based on the approach: prototype clusters use a small set of prototypes (or parameters like mean vector and covariance matrix in mixture models); SOM uses two-dimensional plots; and graph- or density-based approaches typically describe clusters as sets of cluster members.
Intra-cluster distance, also referred to as intra-cluster dissimilarity, measures the proximity of objects within the same cluster.
In the context of K-means clustering, this is measured by the summation of distances between the objects and the centroid of the cluster to which they are assigned.
A cluster centroid is defined as the mean value of the objects in that cluster.
In K-means clustering, the distance between a centroid and an object is denoted as d(vk, xi), where vk represents the centroid of cluster k and xi represents the object.
The Euclidean distance is used as the distance measure.
The overall objective of clustering is to divide a data set into groups based on the similarity of objects while minimizing the intra-cluster dissimilarity.
In K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI), the process involves iteratively modifying the partition to reduce the sum of the distances for each object from its assigned cluster centroid.
This process terminates when the summation of distances is less than a user-specified threshold (e.g., ε = 100) or when no changes to the centroids occurred in the last iteration.
Inter-cluster distance refers to the proximity or distance between two different clusters, utilizing only cross-cluster pairs.
Different clustering algorithms and evaluation measures define this distance differently
In the CURE algorithm, the distance between two clusters is defined as the minimum distance between any two representative points after those points have been shrunk toward their respective centers.
The distance from a point x to another cluster Y is the average distance from x to the members of cluster Y.
b(x) = smallest average distance from x to another cluster
In agglomerative hierarchical clustering, the distance between two clusters is reflected by the height at which they are merged in a dendrogram.
Other methods for computing distance between clusters include using the diameter (variance) of the merged cluster or using summary statistics as defined by BIRCH.
Clustering and classification are both processes used to divide objects into groups, but they differ in how those groups are established and used.
Clustering is the process of dividing objects into groups based on common characteristics; these groups are conceptually meaningful and are referred to as clusters.
In the context of data analysis, clusters are viewed as potential classes, and cluster analysis is the study of techniques used to find these classes automatically.
Classification is the process of assigning particular objects to these established groups.
While clustering can be seen as a form of classification because it creates labels for objects, it is distinguished by the fact that it derives these labels solely from the data.
In contrast, standard classification assigns a class label to new, unlabeled objects using a model that was developed from objects with known class labels.
For this reason, cluster analysis is sometimes called unsupervised classification.
A core point is a point located in the interior of a density-based cluster.
core points are characterized as strongly belonging to one cluster
A point is defined as a core point if there are at least MinPts points within a distance of Eps, where the count includes the point itself.
MinPts and Eps are user-specified parameters, with MinPts typically being greater than or equal to 7
any two core points that are within a distance Eps of one another are placed in the same cluster
a core point can directly reach a border point, though a border point cannot reach back as a core-expanding point
A border point is a point that is not a core point because it does not have enough points in its neighborhood to meet the core point criteria, but it falls within the neighborhood of a core point.
a border point is located on the edge of a dense region
any border point that is close enough to a core point is placed in the same cluster as that core point
a border point belongs to a cluster, it does not expand the cluster because direct density-reachability requires the starting point to be a core point
a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point
Assignment can become ambiguous if a border point is close to core points from different clusters, creating a border tie
common implementation conventions include assigning the border point to the first cluster that reaches it, or using a nearest-core rule as a deterministic tie-breaker
A noise point is any point that is neither a core point nor a border point.
In the context of density-based clustering, these points are located in sparsely occupied or low-density regions.
Within the DBSCAN algorithm, noise points are discarded and ignored by the cluster structure.
The algorithm automatically classifies low-density points as noise and removes them from the clustering process.
The classification of points as noise is sensitive to the algorithm's parameters.
If the epsilon (ε) threshold is too small, most neighborhoods become too small, causing many points to become noise.
If the minPts parameter is too large, real small clusters may disappear as they are classified as noise.
DBSCAN utilizes two user-specified global parameters: Eps (also denoted as ε) and MinPts.
These parameters are used to estimate density by counting points within a radius of Eps, and this count includes the point itself.
MinPts is defined as the minimum number of points required inside the ε-neighborhood for a point to be classified as a core point.
A point is considered a core point if there are at least MinPts within a distance of Eps.
To determine suitable values for these parameters, a basic approach involves analyzing the k-dist, which is the distance from a point to its k-th nearest neighbor.

The procedure is as follows: 1. Compute the k-dist for all data points for a chosen value of k. 2. Sort these k-dist values in increasing order. 3. Plot the sorted values. 4. Identify the value at which there is a sharp change or increase in the plot; this value corresponds to a suitable Eps. 5. Set the value of k used in the process as the MinPts parameter.
Under this selection method, points with a k-dist less than Eps are labeled as core points, while others are labeled as noise or border points.
DBSCAN may fail or have trouble when the density of clusters varies widely because it uses one global density threshold.
In such cases, an Eps threshold that allows the algorithm to find lower-density clusters as distinct may cause higher-density clusters and their surrounding noise to merge into a single cluster.
Conversely, an Eps threshold that separates higher-density clusters may cause lower-density clusters to be marked as noise.
A point q is directly density-reachable from a point p if q is within the epsilon-neighborhood of p (q ∈ N_{ε}(p)) and p is a core point.
Direct density-reachability is directional.

While a core point can directly reach a border point, a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point because the starting point must be a core point for direct density-reachability to occur.

A point q is density-reachable from a point p if there exists a chain of points starting at p and ending at q, denoted as p = p1, p2, ..., pn = q, such that every subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the previous point.
a point pi+1 is directly density-reachable from pi if pi is a core point and q is within the epsilon-neighborhood of p, expressed as q ∈ Nε(p).
To determine if q is density-reachable from p, the following conditions must be met for each step in the chain
This concept assumes that the entire dataset can be evaluated using a single density standard.
Two points, p and q, are considered density-connected if there exists a third point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o.
This concept is used in density-based clustering models, such as DBSCAN, to identify connected dense regions.
Unlike centroid-based partitions that may cut through curved dense shapes, DBSCAN can follow these dense connected regions provided the parameters are suitable.
DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that identifies clusters as regions of high density separated by regions of low density.

Unlike prototype-based methods like K-means, DBSCAN uses a density-based concept to define clusters, allowing it to handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes and making it relatively resistant to noise.

As a partitional clustering algorithm, DBSCAN assigns each object to a single cluster, but it does not produce a complete clustering because points in low-density regions are classified as noise and omitted.
The number of clusters is automatically determined by the algorithm based on a single density threshold, rather than being specified as a parameter in advance.

The algorithm forms clusters through the following procedure: 1. Connect core points that are within a distance Eps of one another into the same cluster. 2. Attach border points to the same cluster as any core point they are close enough to (ties are resolved if a border point is close to core points from different clusters). 3. Discard noise points.
DBSCAN is particularly effective when the natural clusters in the data are noisy, non-spherical, and density-separated, or when the number of clusters is unknown.

However, it can be computationally expensive when calculating nearest neighbors requires all pairwise proximities, and it struggles with high-dimensional data where density is more difficult to define.
DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that is relatively resistant to noise and capable of identifying clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes.
Because of these properties, it can find many clusters that cannot be discovered using K-means.
DBSCAN is most effective when the density-cluster assumption or density connectivity is the appropriate model for the data.
K-means is better suited for data where clusters are compact, centroid-like, and every point should be assigned to a cluster.
DBSCAN has several limitations.
It struggles with high-dimensional data because density is more difficult to define in such spaces.
Additionally, it has difficulty handling data that contains clusters of widely different densities.
DBSCAN can be expensive when the computation of nearest neighbors requires calculating all pairwise proximities, which is typically the case for high-dimensional data.

Internal indices, also known as unsupervised measures of cluster validity, are evaluation measures used to judge the goodness or quality of a clustering structure without relying on external information.
These indices use only the information present within the data set itself.
Unsupervised measures of cluster validity are typically divided into two classes:
Measures of cluster cohesion (also referred to as compactness or tightness), which determine how closely related the objects within a single cluster are.
Measures of cluster separation (also referred to as isolation), which determine how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters.
Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) is an unsupervised internal index used to measure the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external information.
It specifically serves as a centroid-quality measure, evaluating how tightly points sit around their assigned centroids and how well those final centroids represent their assigned points.
A smaller SSE indicates that points are closer to their centroids.
SSE = ∑i=1K ∑x∈Ci (ci - x)²
SSE = ∑i=1K ∑x∈Ci dist(ci, x)²
In these expressions, K represents the number of clusters, Ci is the i-th cluster, and ci is the centroid of that cluster.
Total SSE is the sum of the SSE contributed by each individual cluster.

Because K-means typically converges to a local minimum, various techniques can be used to improve SSE without increasing the number of clusters, such as employing alternate cluster splitting and merging phases to escape local minima.
SSE is used as the objective function for traditional K-means, where the goal is to minimize SSE.
It can also be used as a relative measure to compare different clusterings.
However, SSE is not a density-cluster quality measure.
While increasing the number of clusters (K) almost always reduces SSE—reaching 0 if every point is its own cluster (K=n)—this is often useless for practical clustering.
In contexts like clustering for summarization, the goal may be to reduce SSE to a specific approximation level rather than finding the natural cluster structure.
Cohesion (also referred to as compactness or tightness) is an unsupervised internal measure of cluster validity that determines how closely related the objects within a single cluster are.
It measures the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external information.
Cohesion can be expressed in different ways depending on the clustering approach:
cohesion(Ci) = ∑ x ∈ Ci proximity(x, ci)
where Ci is the cluster and ci is its prototype.
cohesion(Ci) = ∑ x ∈ Ci y ∈ Ci proximity(x, y)
Total Cohesion = ∑ i=1 to K ∑ x ∈ Ci cosine(x, ci)
When using similarity measures, higher values indicate better cohesion; conversely, when using dissimilarity measures, lower values are better.
For Euclidean distance, minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE) is equivalent to maximizing separation (SSB), as the sum of total SSE and total SSB is a constant.
Cohesion is used to evaluate the quality of individual clusters or the overall clustering structure.
A cluster with high cohesion is generally considered better.
If a cluster is not sufficiently cohesive, it may be split into subclusters.
Objects that contribute more to the overall cohesion are typically located in the interior of the cluster, while those contributing less are near the edge.
Separation (also referred to as isolation) is an internal cluster validity measure used to determine how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from others.
It is based on the pairwise distances or similarities between clusters.

For graph-based clusters, separation between two clusters C_i and C_j is the sum of the pairwise similarities of all objects in C_i with all objects in C_j: $$mathsf{separation}(C_i, C_j) = sum x in C_i y in C_j mathsf{proximity}(x, y)$$

For prototype-based clusters (such as those in K-Means), where c_i is the prototype of cluster C_i and c is the overall prototype, separation is measured as: 1. The proximity between two cluster prototypes: $mathsf{separation}(C_i, C_j) = mathsf{proximity}(c_i, c_j)$
2. The proximity between a cluster prototype and the overall prototype: $mathsf{separation}(C_i) = mathsf{proximity}(c_i, c)$

Additionally, separation for a cluster Y can be calculated as the average normalized distance from its center to the centers of all other clusters Y' in the set of clusters zeta: $$operatorname{separation}(Y) = frac{1}{|zeta| - 1} sum_{Y' in zeta, Y' neq Y} d_N(center(Y), center(Y'))$$
When using a proximity function, the interpretation of the result depends on whether the function measures similarity or dissimilarity.
For similarity, lower values are better for separation; for dissimilarity, higher values are better for separation.
The silhouette coefficient is an internal cluster evaluation measure and index that does not use class labels.
It evaluates whether a point is closer to its own cluster than to the nearest competing cluster by incorporating both cohesion (compactness) and separation.

b(x) is the smallest average distance from point x to another cluster.

To evaluate a clustering overall, the average silhouette coefficient of a cluster is the average of the coefficients of its points.
An overall measure of clustering goodness is obtained by computing the average silhouette coefficient of all points in the dataset.

This measure is used to determine the number of clusters; when used with partitional algorithms like K-means, the measure typically decreases until the natural set of clusters is found and increases once clusters are split too finely.
It can also serve as a test statistic in statistical testing to measure the significance of a discovered clustering against a null hypothesis of random partitioning.
While it performs well regarding noise and differing sizes and density, it does not perform well for continuity- or density-based clusters or arbitrary shapes.
Models of Randomness (Approach 1) involves a probabilistic perspective on evaluation.
the use of randomness is beneficial because it ensures that the trees involved are different from one another
Models of Randomness (Approach 2) involves the use of randomization methods to create diverse classifiers.
Many learning algorithms can be manipulated so that applying the same algorithm multiple times to the same training data results in the construction of different classifiers.
an ensemble can be constructed by injecting randomness into the tree-growing procedure.
This injection of randomness is beneficial because it ensures that the resulting trees are different from one another.
Entropy is a supervised index used to measure how well cluster labels match externally supplied class labels.
As an external index, it uses information not present in the data set to measure the extent to which a clustering structure discovered by an algorithm matches an external structure.
Entropy = −∑i=0c⁻1pi(t) log2pi(t)
Entropy(D) = −p+ log2(p+) −p⁻log2(p⁻)
Entropy can be used as a test statistic in statistical testing procedures to measure the significance of a discovered clustering.
In this context, it is compared against a null distribution based on the null hypothesis that no cluster structure exists and the algorithm is producing a random partitioning of the data.
Purity is an external clustering validity index used to measure the extent to which a discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, typically known class labels.
It specifically quantifies the degree to which a cluster contains objects of a single class.
The purity of a cluster i is defined as the fraction of that cluster consisting of objects of a specified class, calculated as: purity(i) = max_j p_{ij}
The overall purity of a clustering is the weighted average over clusters, expressed as: purity = ∑_{i=1}^K m_i * purity(i)
In this context, p_{ij} is computed as m_{ij} / m_i.
Purity is categorized as an external index because it requires the use of true class labels for its computation.

It is used as a classification-oriented measure to evaluate clustering significance, and can serve as a test statistic in statistical testing procedures to determine if a clustering is significant compared to a null hypothesis of random partitioning.

The Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient are similarity-oriented external validation measures used to evaluate the extent to which a discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, typically known class labels.
They are categorized as similarity-oriented because they evaluate the clustering by comparing pairs of objects.

The Rand Index includes these f00 pairs in its calculation, whereas the Jaccard Coefficient ignores f00 and focuses exclusively on pairs that are placed together in at least one of the two structures.
In practice, these indices can be computed using class similarity and cluster similarity matrices.
given values f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Rand statistic is calculated as (2+4)/10=0.6
the Jaccard coefficient is calculated as 2/(2+2+2)=0.33
Precision measures the precision of a cluster with respect to a specific class.
The precision of cluster i with respect to class j is defined by the formula precision(i,j)=pij.
In contexts involving fraudulent transaction detection, the metric is influenced by the percentage of fraudulent transactions in the data, denoted as α.

When data is highly skewed—for example, when α is 2×10−5 in fifty thousand transactions—the precision can be low (e.g., 0.167), indicating that only a small fraction of alarms (such as one in six) are true anomalies.

External Index: Recall is a classification-oriented external index used to measure the extent to which a discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, which is typically known class labels.
Specifically, it quantifies the extent to which a cluster contains all objects of a specified class.
The recall of cluster i with respect to class j is calculated using the formula: recall(i,j) = mij / mj
where mj is the number of objects in class j.
The F-measure is a classification-oriented external index used to measure the extent to which a discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, typically known class labels.
Specifically, it measures the extent to which a cluster contains all objects of a particular class and only objects of that class.
F(i,j) = (2 * precision(i,j) * recall(i,j)) / (precision(i,j) + recall(i,j))
This metric represents a combination of both precision and recall.
A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram used to graphically display a hierarchical clustering.
It illustrates the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which clusters were either merged, in an agglomerative view, or split, in a divisive view.
In a dendrogram, the height at which two clusters are merged reflects the distance between those two clusters.
Dendrograms are used to visualize the nested hierarchy of clusters.
They can be used to generate K clusters by taking the clusters at the Kth level of the dendrogram, where the root is at level 1.
To obtain a final flat clustering from a dendrogram, it must be cut at a specific point.
When drawing a dendrogram by hand, the vertical merge heights and the nested structure are the critical elements; the exact horizontal spacing is not important.
Additionally, while the nested structure must be preserved, branches can be flipped left-to-right.
Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that splits clusters downward.
It begins with all objects contained in a single cluster and repeatedly splits these clusters into smaller ones until a stopping rule is reached or the process results in singleton clusters.
This approach can be particularly useful when a good splitter is available or if the top-level split is meaningful.
In cases where the dataset is very large, divisive techniques may be preferred over agglomerative hierarchical clustering, though some divisive methods still have limits based on dataset size.
Minimum Spanning Tree (MST): This technique starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters.
It is the divisive analog to single link agglomerative clustering and produces the same clustering result.
Bisecting K-means: This is another divisive technique that works for many datasets, although it may encounter problems if the dataset is too large to be contained completely in memory.

MIN (Single Linkage) is a version of hierarchical clustering where the proximity between two clusters is defined as the minimum distance (or maximum similarity) between any two points belonging to the two different clusters.
Visually, this is described as using the nearest bridge; two clusters are considered close if at least one point in one cluster is close to at least one point in the other.
dsingle(Ci, Cj) = min x∈Ci,y∈Cj d(x, y)
The distance between two clusters, Ci and Cj, is expressed by the formula: dsingle(Ci, Cj) = min x∈Ci,y∈Cj d(x, y)

In terms of graph terminology, the procedure involves starting with all points as singleton clusters and adding links between points one at a time, prioritizing the shortest links first, which then combine the points into clusters.
For implementation, the original point-distance matrix can be computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using the minimum value.
Single linkage is effective at handling non-elliptical shapes, but it is sensitive to noise and outliers.

MAX (Complete Linkage) is a version of hierarchical clustering where the proximity between two clusters is defined as the maximum distance (or minimum similarity) between any two points located in the two different clusters.
In this approach, two clusters are considered close only if even the farthest cross-cluster pair is not too far.

Using graph terminology, if the process begins with all points as singleton clusters and links are added between points one at a time (shortest links first), a group of points does not become a cluster until all points within it are completely linked, forming a clique.
To implement this, the original point-distance matrix is computed once.
After a merge occurs, the current matrix is updated using the max operator.
Complete linkage favors globular shapes and is less susceptible to noise and outliers than some alternatives, though it can break large clusters.

Group average linkage is a graph-based approach to hierarchical clustering that defines the proximity between two clusters as the average of all pairwise proximities (or average length of edges) between all pairs of points from the different clusters.

In the context of agglomerative clustering, this method bases its notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between two clusters, such as the pairwise similarity of points within those clusters.
There is a weighted version of group average known as WPGMA.
In WPGMA, the coefficients are constants that are independent of the cluster sizes, specifically: alpha A = 1/2, alpha B = 1/2, beta = 0, and gamma = 0.
Generally, unweighted approaches are preferred unless there is a specific reason to believe that individual points should have different weights.
Like single link and complete link methods, group average linkage is potentially less problematic when dealing with outliers.

Outliers or small groups of outliers tend to form singleton or small clusters that do not merge with other clusters until much later in the merging process, allowing them to be removed by discarding these small clusters.
Hierarchical clustering complexity refers to the computational and storage requirements of the algorithm, which severely limit the size of data sets that can be processed.
For the basic agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithm, space complexity is O(m^2), where m is the number of data points.

This is because the algorithm uses a proximity matrix to store proximities (assuming the matrix is symmetric), and the space needed to track clusters is proportional to the number of clusters, excluding singleton clusters.
Time complexity for this algorithm is O(m^2 log m).
This is derived from the process where m clusters exist at the start and two are merged during each iteration.
If a linear search of the proximity matrix is used, finding the two closest clusters in the ith iteration requires O((m-i+1)^2) time, and updating the proximity matrix requires O(m-i+1) time.
While using a sorted list or heap can reduce the cost of finding the closest clusters, the overall time complexity remains O(m^2 log m).
These prohibitive time and space complexities make hierarchical clustering impractical for large data sets.

To address these issues, data can be partially clustered first using another technique, such as K-means, or scalable alternatives like the bisecting K-means algorithm can be used to produce a hierarchical clustering.
K-Means is a centroid-based, partitional clustering algorithm that directly divides data into K clusters, where each cluster is represented by a centroid.
A centroid is the representative center of a cluster and is a mean position that does not necessarily have to be one of the original data points.
For Euclidean K-Means, the centroid is the mean of all points in the cluster.
$$c_i =  frac{1}{m_i}  sum_{x in C_i} x$$
$$c_i = left( frac{sum{x}}{m_i}, frac{sum{y}}{m_i} right)$$

The algorithm follows these steps in order: 1. Choose the number of clusters K, which is a user-specified parameter. 2. Choose K initial centroids. 3. Assign each point to the nearest centroid; each collection of points assigned to a centroid forms a cluster. 4. Update each centroid by recomputing it as the mean of the points assigned to it. 5. Repeat the assignment and update steps until no point changes clusters, or equivalently, until the centroids stop changing.
K-Means is used to find a specific number of clusters, but when K is large, calculating the distance of each point to each cluster centroid at each iteration can be very expensive.
Additionally, while random initialization is simple and often used, it can result in a clustering that represents a local minimum in terms of the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE).
The SSE Optimization Criterion treats clustering as an optimization problem where the objective is to minimize the total Sum of Squared Error (SSE).
To find a global optimum for this objective function, one would need to enumerate all possible ways of dividing points into clusters and select the set that minimizes the total SSE.
However, this exhaustive strategy is computationally infeasible, making the general clustering problem for a 'minimize SSE' objective computationally infeasible.
Because of this infeasibility, practical approaches are used that may find solutions that are not guaranteed to be optimal.
These solutions can result in a global minimum of the SSE or a suboptimal clustering that is only a local minimum.
In the context of agglomerative hierarchical clustering, a local 'minimize squared error' criterion is used in Ward's method to decide which clusters to merge.
However, because merge decisions in agglomerative clustering cannot be undone, this local optimization does not become a global optimization criterion.

Consequently, clusters at each level in Ward's method do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE, and points in one cluster may be closer to the centroid of a different cluster than to their own.
Despite this, Ward's method is often used to initialize K-means clustering, suggesting a connection between the local and global 'minimize squared error' objective functions.
K-means complexity refers to the space and time requirements of the basic K-means algorithm.
The space requirements are modest because the algorithm only stores the centroids and the data points.
The storage required is O((m+K)n), where m is the number of points, K is the number of clusters, and n is the number of attributes.
The time requirements are also modest and are basically linear in the number of data points.
The time required is O(I * K * m * n), where I is the number of iterations required for convergence, K is the number of clusters, m is the number of points, and n is the number of attributes.
K-means is linear in the number of points (m) and is considered efficient and simple provided that the number of clusters (K) is significantly less than the number of points (m).
Centroid initialization sensitivity refers to the impact that the selection of initial centroids has on the final clustering results in K-means.
standard K-means can be susceptible to initialization problems
selecting initial centroids are used to improve results and lower the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE)
One approach for selecting initial centroids involves selecting the first point at random or using the centroid of all points.
Each subsequent initial centroid is then selected as the point farthest from any of the already selected initial centroids.

This ensures the initial centroids are well separated, though it can lead to the selection of outliers rather than points in dense regions, potentially reducing the number of centroids available for the majority of points.
To mitigate this and reduce computational expense, this method is often applied to a random sample of the points.
K-means++ picks centroids incrementally until k centroids are selected.
each point has a probability of being picked as the new centroid that is proportional to the square of its distance to its closest centroid
This method is guaranteed to find a solution that is optimal to within a factor of O log(k)
resulting in noticeably better clustering results in terms of lower SSE
bisecting K-means is a variant that is less susceptible to initialization problems
This is because it only uses two centroids at each step and performs several trial bisections, selecting the one with the lowest SSE
Traditional K-means has several limitations regarding the types of clusters it can effectively detect.
It is sensitive to outliers and struggles to identify 'natural' clusters when they possess non-spherical or non-globular shapes, or when clusters exhibit widely different densities or sizes.

Specific failure cases include situations where a cluster is significantly larger than others, causing the larger cluster to be broken while a smaller cluster is combined with a portion of the larger one.
Similarly, K-means may fail if some clusters are much denser than others, or it may produce clusters that mix portions of natural clusters if those natural clusters are not globular.
Additionally, K-means requires a meaningful mean and a meaningful distance to function; consequently, it cannot be used with raw categories as they do not have meaningful averages.

From an optimization perspective, K-means can be limited by reaching a local minimum, where the algorithm cannot improve from its current path, as opposed to a global minimum where no possible clustering with the same K has a lower total SSE.
Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm and a straightforward extension of the basic K-means algorithm.
It is characterized as a hierarchical sequence of binary splits.

The algorithm follows these steps: 1. Start with one cluster containing all points. 2. Select one existing cluster to split. 3. Apply basic K-Means with K = 2 to that selected cluster to split it into two subclusters. 4. Often, this split is repeated several times with different initializations, and the split with the lowest total SSE is kept. 5. Replace the original cluster with the two new clusters. 6. Repeat this process until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached.
Bisecting K-Means is used to produce better-quality clusterings with lower SSE and is less susceptible to initialization problems than standard K-Means.
This is because it only considers two centroids at each step and can perform trial bisections to select the best one.

Additionally, it can run significantly faster than regular K-means because, except for the first step, it only computes the distance of a subset of points to the two centroids being considered, thereby reducing the total number of similarities computed.
While Bisecting K-Means is a valid algorithm on its own and useful for taxonomies or broad-to-specific segmentation, it makes local split decisions.

Therefore, if the goal is a flat clustering with lower total SSE, the final bisecting centroids can be used as initial centroids for a standard K-Means refinement step, which allows every point to be compared against every final centroid.

Euclidean distance is a distance metric used as a proximity measure between instances, specifically for data points in Euclidean space and many types of dense, continuous data.
It compares locations rather than direction or pattern.
It is a specific case of an Lp norm distance and is included within the class of proximity measures known as Bregman divergence (specifically squared Euclidean distance).
Positivity: d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y, and d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y.

Euclidean distance is commonly used in literature for proximity measures.
In clustering, it is used to determine the closest centroid for a data point.
For example, in K-means, the sum of squared error (SSE), also known as scatter, is calculated by summing the squared Euclidean distances from each data point to its closest centroid.

While it is effective for uncorrelated attributes, it may be less suitable than Mahalanobis distance for data where attributes are correlated, as Mahalanobis distance gives less emphasis to the direction of largest variance.
Cosine similarity is a similarity score used to measure the cosine of the angle between two vectors, x and y.
Unlike distance measures, a larger cosine similarity score indicates that the objects are more similar.
When the cosine similarity is 1, the vectors point in the same direction and are the same except for their length.
A score of 0 indicates that the vectors are perpendicular and do not share any terms or words.
A score of -1 indicates that the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.
Cosine similarity does not take the length of the two data objects into account when computing similarity.
For vectors that have already been normalized to a length of 1, the measure can be calculated by taking a simple inner product.
Normalizing objects to unit length can reduce the time required when computing many cosine similarities.
This measure is particularly useful for sparse data, such as documents represented as document-term matrices, where it compares direction or pattern rather than location.
It is also a member of the class of proximity measures known as Bregman divergence, allowing it to be used as the basis for K-means style clustering algorithms where the cluster centroid is the mean.
The Rand Index is a similarity-oriented external validation measure used to evaluate clustering by comparing the resulting cluster structure against true class labels.
It assesses how closely the cluster labels match the class labels by comparing pairs of objects.
The Rand Index is defined by the following formula: $$Rand Index = frac{f_{11} + f_{00}}{f_{11} + f_{10} + f_{01} + f_{00}}
In this formula, $f_{00}$ represents the pairs of objects that are correctly separated in both the clustering and the class structure.
To compute the Rand Index, class similarity and cluster similarity matrices are used.
The calculation only counts pairs of distinct objects; it does not count the diagonal elements of the matrices.
The Rand Index is used when external labels are available for evaluation.
Once cluster assignments and class labels are known, the original feature values are no longer needed for the calculation.

It differs from the Jaccard Coefficient in that the Rand Index includes $f_{00}$ (correctly separated pairs), whereas Jaccard ignores $f_{00}$ and focuses only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
The Jaccard coefficient (often symbolized by j) is a similarity measure used to determine the similarity between two binary vectors.
It is frequently employed to handle objects consisting of asymmetric binary attributes, such as transactions in a matrix where a 1 indicates an item was purchased and a 0 indicates it was not.
$$Jaccard Coefficient =  f_{11} / (f_{11} + f_{10} + f_{01})$$
In this calculation, the measure ignores $f_{00}$ and focuses exclusively on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
Beyond pairs of binary variables, the Jaccard coefficient can be extended to more than two variables by using frequency tables tabulated in a multidimensional contingency table.
Additionally, an extended Jaccard coefficient (represented as $varepsilon J$ or $EJ$) exists for document data, which reduces to the standard Jaccard coefficient when binary attributes are used.
In the context of cluster validity, the Jaccard coefficient is one of the most frequently used supervised measures.
Compared to the Rand statistic, the Jaccard coefficient is considered stricter.
A similarity matrix is a matrix used to represent the degree to which pairs of objects in a data set are alike, where higher values indicate greater similarity.
Similarities are typically non-negative and often range between 0 (no similarity) and 1 (complete similarity).

An ideal cluster similarity matrix is constructed by creating a matrix with one row and one column for each data point and assigning a 1 to an entry if the associated pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise.

When the rows and columns are sorted so that objects in the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, where entries are 1 inside the blocks (representing intra-cluster similarity) and 0 elsewhere.
To visualize or judge a clustering, a similarity matrix can be ordered with respect to cluster labels and then plotted.
The patterns revealed in such a matrix can illustrate the separation of clusters.

Similarity matrices are used to evaluate the goodness of clustering by calculating the correlation between an actual similarity matrix and an ideal version based on cluster labels.

Additionally, they are used in the Rand and Jaccard indices, which compare a cluster similarity matrix against a class similarity matrix (where an entry is 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise).
In these comparisons, diagonal entries—which compare a point with itself—are not counted because only pairs of distinct objects are considered.
Missing values occur when attribute values or entire data objects are absent from a dataset.
This can happen because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects.
Missing values are considered a data quality issue related to measurement and collection and must be accounted for during data analysis.

Naïve Bayes classifiers can handle missing values in the training set by ignoring them when computing conditional probability estimates, and in test instances by using only non-missing attribute values for posterior probabilities.

Bayesian networks can handle missing values during both training and testing; for test instances, they perform inference by treating the missing attribute as an unobserved node and marginalizing out its effect on the target class.

Decision tree classifiers employ several methods for test sets: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on the probability of the missing attribute's value; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a non-missing surrogate attribute that resembles the missing attribute's partitions; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value.
Logistic regression and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) cannot handle instances with missing values in the training or testing phase.
For logistic regression, training instances with missing values can be discarded, but missing values in a test instance will cause the model to fail to predict the class label.
General strategies for dealing with missing values include data preprocessing steps such as discarding instances or attributes with missing values, or using imputation.

Imputation involves estimating missing data, such as using interpolation for smooth time series or using the average (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes) of nearest neighbors.
Additionally, similarity calculations for clustering can be performed using only the attributes that are not missing, though this results in an approximate similarity.
A missingness mechanism refers to the underlying process or distribution that leads to the introduction of missing values (MVs) in a dataset.

Categorizing these mechanisms is important because the assumptions made about the missingness mechanism, along with the pattern of missing values, can determine which treatment method can be correctly applied.
One specific mechanism is Missing At Random (MAR).

Informally, data is MAR when the probability that an observation is missing may depend on the observed part of the data (Xobs) but not on the missing part (Xmis), where the total data X is composed of X = (Xobs, Xmis).
In a MAR mechanism, given specific values for features in Xobs, the distribution of the remaining features is the same for both observed and missing cases.
This mechanism can be represented by a probability model for a matrix B, where B contains variables with values of 1 or 0 indicating whether X elements are observed or missing, respectively.
The distribution of B is related to X and unknown parameters ζ, described by P(B|X, ζ).
Under the MAR assumption, this distribution does not depend on Xmis, expressed as: P(B|Xobs, Xmis, ζ) = P(B|Xobs, ζ)
Multiple Imputation (MI) should only be applied when either MCAR or MAR missingness mechanisms hold.
The deletion strategy is a simple and effective approach for handling missing values by eliminating the affected components of a data set.
This strategy can be applied in two ways: eliminating data objects that contain missing values or eliminating attributes that contain missing values.
Omitting objects with missing values may be expedient if the data set contains only a few such objects.

However, this can be problematic if many objects have missing values, as even partially specified objects contain some information, and excessive deletion can make a reliable analysis difficult or impossible.
Eliminating attributes with missing values should be performed with caution, as the attributes being removed may be critical to the analysis.
Imputation is the process of replacing missing values (MVs) in a dataset.
In the context of incomplete objects, the goal is to obtain values for non-reference attributes, where reference attributes are those whose values are available for a given object.
Imputation methods can be categorized by their theoretical origin.
Statistical methods model relationships between values by searching for hidden distribution probabilities.
Machine learning (ML) methods use models to infer implicit information and predict missing values, similar to how regression or classification predicts continuous or nominal values.
ML methods alleviate the need to search for an estimated underlying distribution of the data, though they are still subject to the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption for correct application.
From an unsupervised perspective, the best imputation methods generate values closest to the true but unknown missing values.
This is often quantified using mean square error (MSE) or root mean square error (RMSE).
In supervised paradigms, such as classification, a good imputation method is one that enables the classifier to achieve better accuracy, which can be measured using Wilson’s Noise Ratio.
Data integration is the process of gathering and merging data elements from several or heterogeneous sources, such as different databases, into a single data set.
This process is necessary when data comes from diverse sources that may have different table schemes or attribute names, which can produce uneven examples that require consolidation.
Additionally, inconsistencies may arise when attribute values represent the same concept but use different names.
A critical component of the integration process is the creation of a data map.
This map establishes how each instance should be arranged within a common structure to represent a real-world example.
In the case of relational databases, data is typically flattened and gathered into a single record.
While some database frameworks provide in-database access utilities to traverse the database via a map, extracting the data to an external file is generally the preferred option for preprocessing.

This is because preprocessing is time-consuming; keeping data in the database requires repeated application of preprocessing, whereas an external file allows for faster processing and modeling if the data fits in memory and is already preprocessed.
If data integration is not performed properly, the resulting data set may contain redundancies and inconsistencies, such as redundant and correlated attributes or inconsistent and duplicated tuples.
These issues can decrease the accuracy and speed of subsequent data mining processes.
Automatic approaches for integration exist in literature, ranging from techniques that match and find schemas to procedures that reconcile different schemas.
Correctly integrated data is not necessarily free from errors; integration can result in a high proportion of dirty data, including missing data, wrong data, and non-standard representations.
Such dirty data can lead to unreliable models, with the degree of impact varying by the specific data mining algorithm used.
An attribute is considered redundant when it can be derived from another attribute or a set of other attributes.
Redundancy can also be caused by inconsistencies in attribute names or dimensions.
Redundant attributes are characterized by being strongly correlated with other attributes in the data.

Redundancy is a problem to be avoided because it typically increases the size of the data set, which in turn increases the modeling time for data mining algorithms and may induce overfitting in the resulting model.

In high-dimensional settings, a large number of redundant attributes can make models like logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) susceptible to overfitting, leading to poor generalization performance.

Additionally, in nearest neighbor classifiers, a large number of highly correlated redundant attributes can bias proximity measures, resulting in improper distance estimates and adversely affecting performance.
Redundancies can be detected using correlation analysis to measure the strength of the implication of one attribute on another.
For nominal attributes with a finite set of values, the chi-squared (χ2) test is commonly applied.

The process involves: 1. Creating a contingency table of joint events (Ai, Bj), where attribute A takes value ai and attribute B takes value bj. 2. Computing the chi-squared statistic using the formula: χ2 = Σ Σ ((oij - eij)^2 / eij), where oij is the observed frequency of the joint event (Ai, Bj) and eij is the expected frequency. 3. Calculating the expected frequency as: eij = (count(A = ai) × count(B = bj)) / m, where m is the number of instances in the data set, count(A = ai) is the number o

eij = (count(A = ai) × count(B = bj)) / m

If the significance level is below the established one (or the computed value is above the table value), the null hypothesis of independence is rejected, and the attributes are statistically correlated.
For numeric attributes, the correlation coefficient and covariance are typically used.
r_{A,B} = (Σ (ai - A_mean)(bi - B_mean)) / (m * σA * σB) = (Σ (ai * bi) - m * A_mean * B_mean) / (m * σA * σB)

Certain algorithms handle redundancy differently: decision trees typically select only one of several redundant attributes because they show similar gains in purity; rule-based classifiers ignore redundant attributes after one has been used as a conjunct because the others show little to no information gain; and linear SVMs, Bayesian networks, and logistic regression can handle redundancy by learning similar weights for duplicate attributes or expressing richer conditional independence.
Duplicate tuples are repeated instances within a dataset.
They can be generated by the use of denormalized tables, which are sometimes employed to increase the speed of join operations.
Duplicate tuples are problematic because they waste computing time and storage space for data mining algorithms and can serve as a source of inconsistency.
Furthermore, if the data integration process is not performed properly, duplicated tuples and redundancies may appear, which decreases the speed and accuracy of subsequent data mining processes.
Some duplicates are harder to detect than others.

While some can be found by simply scanning the dataset for duplicate instances, others result from errors in the entry process where differences in certain attribute values, such as the identifier value, produce identical repeated instances that are nonetheless considered different.
Inconsistent values are data entries that conflict with other related data or established constraints.

These inconsistencies can manifest in several ways: they may occur when attribute values fall outside of an established range (often specified in the data set's associated metadata), or when different sources use different systems of measurement, causing identical instances to remain unidentified.
Another form of inconsistency occurs when related fields contradict one another, such as an address field where the listed zip code area is not contained within the listed city.
Such errors can be caused by human factors, such as an individual transposing two digits or a digit being misread during the scanning of a handwritten form.
Inconsistent values also appear during the detection of duplicate or almost-duplicate data objects.
When two objects represent a single real-world entity, they often have different values for corresponding attributes; these inconsistent values must be resolved to eliminate the duplicates.
It is important to detect and, where possible, correct these problems.
Checking for values outside of established ranges is noted as an easy condition to verify.
Data cleaning is the process of detection and correction of data inaccuracies to remove or repair dirty data.
It is typically performed after data is computer readable and constitutes a unique source, and must be completed before applying any data mining (DM) technique.
Dirty data usually manifests in two forms: missing data and wrong (noisy) data.
The sources of such data include bugs in the data processing system, as well as data entry, update, and transmission errors.
Data cleaning is necessary because a high proportion of dirty data in training or testing sets likely produces a less reliable model.
Without this step, DM algorithms may be unable to handle the data, or the extracted knowledge will be barely accurate.

The impact of dirty data varies by algorithm; for example, distance-based algorithms (such as KNN), Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), and decision trees (particularly those of higher order than two) are known to be susceptible to noise.
It is important to distinguish data cleaning from other preprocessing steps: having a uniform data set without measurable inconsistencies does not mean the data is clean.

Furthermore, achieving a consistent and almost error-free data set does not necessarily mean the data is in the best form for a DM algorithm, as subsequent normalization and transformation may still be required to adapt the data to specific algorithm needs.
Variable transformation refers to a process applied to all values of a variable, where the transformation is applied to the value of the variable for each object.
Examples include simple functional transformations, such as taking the absolute value when only magnitude is important, and normalization.
Normalization is often used to rescale data to the same range of values.
In literature, this usually refers to min-max normalization where the final interval is [0, 1] (meaning new-minA = 0 and new-maxA = 1), though the interval [-1, 1] is also typical.

An equivalent formulation for min-max normalization uses a base value new-minA and a desired new range R, expressed by the formula: ν ^ { ′ } = n e w - m i n _ { A } + R ( ν - m i n _ { A } ) / ( m a x _ { A } - m i n _ { A } )
In this formula, maxA and minA are the original maximum and minimum attribute values, respectively.
Another type of transformation is used to obtain a new variable that is likely to behave like a normally distributed one.
This specific transformation is only recommended when the test and training data are the same, as it cannot be applied separately to the training and test partitions.
These techniques are used to adapt a data set to the needs of a subsequent data mining algorithm.

Normalization is particularly common for learning methods based on distances, as rescaling prevents attributes with large maxA - minA differences from dominating distance calculations and misleading the learning process.
It is also used to speed up the learning process in Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) by helping weights converge faster.
Additionally, transformation or normalization may be required to obtain proper similarity measures, such as when dealing with time series that have periodic patterns or trends.
A confusion matrix is a table used to evaluate the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against the true labels of instances.
It provides a concise representation of classification performance on a given test data set and summarizes the number of instances predicted correctly or incorrectly using four counts.
For binary classification, the matrix consists of the following four counts: - TP (True Positive) - FP (False Positive) - FN (False Negative) - TN (True Negative)
In a typical binary classification layout, rows are used for the true class and columns are used for the predicted class.
While the confusion matrix provides the detailed information needed to determine model performance, it can be difficult to interpret and compare using these four-dimensional representations.
Consequently, these counts are often summarized into single-value evaluation measures, such as accuracy, to make comparing different models more convenient.
However, some measures like accuracy may not be suitable for data sets with imbalanced class distributions.
Accuracy is an evaluation metric used to assess the quality of a classifier or a classification rule.
For a classification rule, accuracy (also known as the confidence factor) is defined as the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels are equal to the rule's predicted label.
$$Accuracy =  rac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$$
$$Accuracy =  rac{ ext{number~of~correct~predictions}}{ ext{number~of~all~predictions}}$$
Measured accuracy is an estimate based on a finite test set and is not guaranteed to be the exact true accuracy of the classifier.
Because it depends on the test sample, accuracy can be misleading, particularly under class imbalance, where it may hide poor performance on the positive class.
To determine if one classifier is significantly better than another, a Z-statistic is used.

A common classroom shortcut for this test is that if the absolute value of the Z-statistic is greater than 1.64 (|Z| > 1.64), the classifier with the higher accuracy wins; otherwise, the result is a draw.

Precision, also referred to as the positive predicted value (PPV), is an evaluation measure defined as the fraction of correct predictions of the positive class over the total number of positive predictions.
Precision, p = TP / (TP + FP)
Precision is a useful measure for highly skewed test sets where positive predictions are small in number but are required to be mostly correct.
A classifier with high precision is likely to have most of its positive predictions correct.
Precision is sensitive to the skew of the data.

Consequently, when using precision to select a score threshold on a validation set, it is necessary to ensure that the skew of the validation set is similar to that of the test set to achieve optimal test performance.
Alternatively, an estimate of the test data skew can be used with the true positive rate (TPR) and true negative rate (TNR) from the validation set to estimate the precision on the test set.
Precision only captures the effect of false positives, not false negatives.
Therefore, optimizing only for precision may result in a classifier that is very conservative in assigning positive labels, leading to high precision but very poor recall.
Recall, also known as sensitivity in the medical community and as the True Positive Rate (TPR), is a metric used to evaluate classifiers.
A classifier that exhibits a high TPR has a high probability of correctly identifying the positive instances within a dataset.
Recall = Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN)
Where TP represents True Positives and FN represents False Negatives.
Specificity, also known as the true negative rate (TNR), is defined as the fraction of negative test instances that are correctly predicted by a classifier.
It specifically checks how many actual negatives were correctly rejected.
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)
In this formula, TN represents true negatives and FP represents false positives.
Specificity is based on actual negatives and uses actual negatives in the denominator.
This distinguishes it from precision for the negative class, as the latter would use predicted negatives in the denominator.
The F-measure is an evaluation measure used to evaluate a match, such as in the context of hierarchical F-measure.
A confusion matrix provides a concise representation of classification performance on a given test data set.

In the context of binary classification, the matrix is a four-dimensional representation consisting of four counts: True Positives (TP), False Negatives (FN), False Positives (FP), and True Negatives (TN).

For binary classifiers, the entire confusion matrix can be computed if the following information is available: the total number of instances (N), the skew factor (α), and the True Positive Rate (TPR) and True Negative Rate (TNR).
The skew among classes is formally defined using P (the number of actual positives) and N (the number of actual negatives).
The evaluation workflow involves the use of multiple evaluation measures to assess a classifier.
Optimizing only a single evaluation measure can lead to suboptimal results, such as a classifier that exhibits low false negatives (FN) but high false positives (FP), or vice versa.
a classifier that declares every instance to be positive will achieve perfect recall, but will simultaneously result in a high false positive rate (FPR) and very poor precision.
A confidence interval for accuracy is an interval of parameter values in which an estimated parameter value is guaranteed to fall a certain percentage of times.

Because accuracy measured on a finite test set is only an estimate, the confidence interval provides a plausible range for the classifier's true accuracy, expressing the uncertainty and sampling noise inherent in the result.
The confidence level is the percentage of times the estimated parameter will fall within the interval.
For example, a 95% confidence level indicates the interval of values that contains 95% of the distribution.
Under the normal approximation, the confidence interval is calculated as the accuracy plus or minus a margin of error (estimate ± uncertainty margin).
For a 90% two-sided interval, the formula uses Z0.95 = 1.64.
Larger test sets produce smaller standard errors, which reduces sampling uncertainty and results in a narrower confidence interval.

Comparing two models on independent test sets involves evaluating a pair of models using two separate, independent test sets to determine if the observed difference in their performance is statistically significant.
The number of instances in the first test set and the second test set are denoted as n1 and n2, respectively.
The error rates for the models on these respective sets are also tracked to test for statistical significance.
a primary difficulty when comparing different classification models is determining whether a difference in observed performance is statistically significant rather than due to chance.
one model might achieve 85% accuracy on a set of 30 instances while another achieves 75% accuracy on a set of 5000 instances.
The significance level, denoted as α, is a fixed constant in hypothesis testing that is decided before any tests are performed.
It represents the probability of incurring a type I error, also known as the type I error rate, and is equal to the probability of the critical region under the null hypothesis.
In practice, a result is considered statistically significant if its p-value is lower than the user-defined significance level α.
Common choices for this level include 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%).

When performing hypothesis tests, rejecting the null hypothesis occurs if the test statistic falls within the critical region, which is equivalent to rejecting the null hypothesis if the p-value falls below the pre-specified threshold α.
For example, in a Chi-square test, independence is rejected if the calculated value exceeds the critical value associated with the chosen significance level.

One-sided and two-sided tests are methods used to determine if an observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis, which is indicated by a low p-value representing smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution.
One-sided tests, which can be right-tailed or left-tailed, are used when testing for a specific direction, such as whether one classifier (A) is better than another (B).
In a one-sided test, all of the 0.05 probability is located in a single tail.
Two-sided tests (also called two-tailed tests) are used to determine if classifiers are different in either direction.
A two-sided test distributes probability across both tails; for example, it may have 0.025 probability in each tail.
For a two-tailed test at α = 0.05, the test normally uses |Z| > 1.96.
For a 90% two-sided interval, the formula uses Z0.95 = 1.64.
The test sample size is a critical parameter that must be chosen after a sampling technique has been selected.
The size of the sample directly influences the representativeness of the data and the reliability of the resulting measurements; specifically, measured accuracy depends on the test sample.

There is a trade-off associated with sample size: larger sample sizes increase the probability that a sample will be representative, but they simultaneously reduce the primary advantages gained from sampling.
Conversely, smaller sample sizes carry the risk that patterns may be missed or that erroneous patterns may be detected.
in a dataset of 8000 two-dimensional points, a sample of 2000 points may preserve most of the data structure, whereas a sample of 500 points may result in much of that structure being missing

in a dataset with 10 clusters, a sample size of 20 provides only a 20% chance of including all clusters, and a sample size of 30 still leaves a moderate chance (nearly 40%) of failing to contain objects from all 10 clusters
An ensemble classifier is a method that combines several base classifiers to produce a single final prediction.
These base classifiers are often individually imperfect, but their combined decision can be more robust than any single classifier.
The basic process involves constructing multiple classifiers from original data and aggregating their predictions when classifying unknown examples.
Base classifiers can be generated either in parallel (all at once) or sequentially (one after another).

In binary classification, this is typically framed as a scenario where the minority class is the positive class and the majority class is the negative class.
Class imbalance poses challenges for classification because many methods only work well when the training set has a balanced representation of both classes.
